fix(assistant-files): make move_to_trash and save_attachment usable (#23598)

### What this PR does

Before this PR: the `assistant-files` server exposed three dead ends.

- `move_to_trash` refused every file in a user workspace stored under
`~/Library/Application Support/…`, because macOS treated all of
`~/Library` as application data. In a four-week audit of Agent sessions,
all 30 recorded calls failed; 28 of them hit this rule.
- `save_attachment` resolved only the hashed `file_<digest>` handle. The
conversation shows the original filename, so all 13 recorded calls
passed a name the tool could never match.
- Both tools replaced the real reason with `Tool execution failed`, so
the model could not tell a protected path from a bad handle or a missing
parent directory.

After this PR:

- macOS application-data containers are the sensitive Library children
(Keychains, LaunchAgents, LaunchDaemons, Preferences, Cookies, Accounts,
Safari, Mail, Messages, Mobile Documents, CloudStorage) plus Cherry
Studio's own `Library/Application Support/CherryStudio`; `app.userdata`
still covers relocated installs. A workspace under `Application Support`
works, while `~/.ssh`, `~/Library/Keychains`, Cherry Studio data,
workspace roots, and version-control metadata stay refused.
- `save_attachment` accepts a unique display filename as an alias for
the handle. A duplicate filename asks for the handle and lists the
candidates instead of guessing.
- `assistant-files` failures return a sanitized reason (control
characters stripped, 500-character cap) so the model can self-correct.

Fixes N/A

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The trash guard's purpose is to keep user data recoverable, not to make
workspace trash operations impossible. Narrowing the macOS container
keeps credential, configuration, and Cherry Studio data protected
without covering the user's chosen workspace. The review-first handle
keeps attachments unambiguous: an alias is only accepted when exactly
one attachment carries that name.

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Other applications' data under `~/Library/Application Support` is no
longer blanket-protected by this guard. The tool only reaches paths the
workspace contains, so the exposure is limited to a workspace rooted
inside that tree.
- A duplicate display name requires the handle; the error lists the
candidates.
- Failure text can include the user-supplied path and the tool's own
reason. It never includes attachment entry ids or temporary copy paths;
`save_attachment` still replaces filesystem failures with a path-based
message.
- Windows keeps the previous behavior: a user workspace under `AppData`
remains refused.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Exempt every strict child of the passed workspace: a workspace rooted
at the app data directory could then trash `cherrystudio.sqlite`;
narrowing `~/Library` keeps Cherry Studio's data protected independently
of the workspace root.
- Inject `file_<digest>` handles into the conversation: the handle is an
internal derivation and the conversation already shows the filename;
teaching the tool the visible name is the smaller change and still
detects ambiguity.
- Keep failures opaque: the audit shows the model cannot self-correct
without the reason; only control characters and length are stripped.

refactor(agent-runtime-pi-durable): resolve child relations from native records (#23772)

### What this PR does

Before this PR: Pi Durable kept a runtime-wide promise cache of child
relations and a task graph watch used only for discovery. Completed
native children could disappear from discovery after restart, and a
failed relation read could remain cached.

After this PR: Parent attachment scans paginated native ownership
records; commit observation delivers new children. Child access and
relation lookup read native creation evidence directly. Pending relation
delivery drains before settlement and shutdown, and failed attachment
can retry cleanly.

Fixes: None.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made: Parent-scoped native reads replace a
second relationship lifecycle. Pending child access skips unrelated text
revisions. Commit listeners read immutable creation records through
owned storage because the SDK forbids calling Session APIs from those
listeners; these reads finish before storage closes.

The following alternatives were considered: Keeping the promise cache
retains failures and duplicates native ownership. Reading only the
projected snapshot can incorrectly reject an already committed child
while delivery is delayed. No replacement manager, SDK patch, dependency
upgrade, public contract change or database migration is introduced.

implementation discussion in the working thread; the durable rationale
is recorded in section 13 of the Agent Note below.

### What this PR does

Before this PR: `ThreadFeed` copied an event into its queue but
delivered a separate, potentially shared `value`. A consumer could
mutate live updates seen by other observers and the stored snapshot. Pi
and Durable also copied their captured batches, duplicating the queue's
unused event copy.

After this PR: `ThreadFeed` synchronously clones the captured delivery
at enqueue time. Queue entries retain a separate close flag instead of
another event payload. Pi and Durable assemble their batches without the
redundant clone; internal baseline/recovery capture avoids an
intermediate snapshot copy.

copies to preserve ownership isolation, while assigning delivery copying
to the feed. Metadata remains captured synchronously with its facts;
overflow retention, callback draining and close ordering retain their
existing contracts.

The following alternatives were considered: Removing all copies would
expose internal state. Keeping copying in each adapter would leave
ordinary `observe()` deliveries unprotected and duplicate the ownership

<!-- Template from
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md?-->

### What this PR does

Before this PR: `TopicMessageProjection.accumulate()` ran the renderer
projection (`projectStreamMessageForRenderer`) on every accepted chunk.
That projection `JSON.stringify`s every finished tool output in the
message to check the 32 KB transport budget, so once a turn has large
tool results, each text chunk re-serializes all of them. The result was
then overwritten by the next chunk before the 80 ms coalescing timer
published it, and the work also ran when no window subscribed to the
topic.

After this PR:
- `MessageProjection.update()` accepts a function and resolves it only
when the batch flushes; `TopicMessageProjection` stores raw messages and
projects them inside that function, so projection runs once per
published batch.
- Without subscribers, non-immediate updates no longer arm the 80 ms
timer; the pending view is resolved by `snapshot()`, which is how a new
subscriber captures its baseline. Terminal publishes stay immediate.
`ChildThreadProjection` only uses immediate updates and is unaffected.
- `execution-overlay.md` documents both rules.

Fixes # N/A

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made: While a window is subscribed,
finished tool outputs are still re-serialized once per flush (at most
every 80 ms) instead of being cached. This removes the per-chunk cost
with a small change and no new state; flush-time cost measured at ~44 ms
per 14 s stream in the scenario below.

The following alternatives were considered: Caching the defer decision
per `toolCallId` and output reference (decide once when the output
becomes available). It would also remove the per-flush cost, but it
needs a part-level projection hook and cache invalidation across
retries; not worth it given the measured residual.

### What this PR does

Every `readEditSnapshotTx` call read the full active path (all message

again via `readForkPrefixTx(messageId)`, whose result is just a prefix

thread.

(`rows.slice(0, index)`) and applies the fork checkpoint mapping through
a shared `applyForkCheckpointsTx`, also used by `readForkPrefixTx`.
- `selectEditParentTx` uses a version-only `readEditVersionTx` and no
longer computes the prefix.
- One edit now does 3 full-path reads instead of 6. The `version` hash
input (`{ source, rows }`) is unchanged, so outstanding edit drafts stay
valid and `history_changed` detection is as strict as before.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

`messageId` is guaranteed to lie on the active path (otherwise the
existing `invalid_target` check throws first), so the path from
`messageId` is exactly the leading slice of the head path; both reads go
through the same CTE, `orderPath`, and root filter.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Replacing the full-content SHA-256 with `ids + updatedAt`: rejected —
it relies on every write bumping `updatedAt` and misses same-millisecond
rewrites, weakening the `history_changed` guard to save one hash pass.
- Moving the read-only snapshot out of `withWriteTx`: no measurable gain
— the main DB is a single synchronous connection, so the cost is
main-thread blocking either way.

attachment and final persistence remain retryable.

explicit handoff/close barriers. Deleted replies cannot reappear through
stale checkpoints or replay.

pending results keep Stop available and append parent summaries to the
same assistant reply. Resident commands do not block replies; missing or
mixed provenance follows the existing independent handoff.

execution. Delete legacy executors, redundant contract fields, unused
driver APIs/helpers and public exports; keep native input ownership,
history, context calculations and charge attribution.

credentials; native response identity can later bind the existing charge
to a product message. Remove the unused billing session column, index,
query and unmerged migration. Unbound calls remain in overall usage;

`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` to `devDependencies`. No release has
shipped since then; the latest tag, v2.1.10, predates both PRs.
- The app shipped two copies of `ai`: `node_modules/ai` (the adapters
load it through `@cherrystudio/agent-runtime`) and a second copy bundled
into main, because `ai` was a `devDependency`. This contradicts the
`pnpm-workspace.yaml` override comment ("the app runs exactly one `ai`
module").

`zipfile`. None of these packages are in the lockfile.

After this PR:

- `ai` and `zod` are in `dependencies` (R4). Main loads the single
shipped `ai` and `zod`, and the adapters load again in a packaged build.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- `ai` is now loaded from `node_modules` instead of the main bundle. It
ships anyway as a dependency of `@cherrystudio/agent-runtime`, so the
package gains no new files and main loses its bundled copy.

because `main.js` requires `ai` and `ai` requires `zod/v4`. Main's own

That check catches this whole class of problem, not only `zod`.

### What this PR does

Before this PR:

`BaseService.registerDisposable` only appended to `_disposables`.
Disposing the returned `Disposable` early (for example
`this.registerInterval(...).dispose()` when an on-demand timer is no
longer needed) ran the cleanup but left the entry in the list until the
service stopped. A service that repeatedly starts and stops a timer
gained one stale entry per cycle.

After this PR:

- A cleanup-function registration (`registerDisposable(fn)`, and so
`registerInterval`, `ipcHandle`, `ipcOn`) removes itself from
`_disposables` when disposed early.
- `_cleanupDisposables` drains the list front to back, so an entry
removing itself during cleanup cannot make the loop skip the next one.
Disposal order is unchanged.

Fixes # N/A

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Only cleanup-function registrations prune themselves.
`registerDisposable(obj)` returns the caller's own object, so it cannot
observe an external `obj.dispose()` without wrapping or patching the
object, which would break the `T` identity return. Every timer and IPC
helper uses the function form, so on-demand timers are covered.
- `_disposables` stays an array (with `indexOf` + `splice`). Lists are
small, and existing tests read `_disposables.length`.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Switching `_disposables` to a `Set`: O(1) delete, but it changes the
internal shape for no measurable gain at these sizes.

#23733, which makes remote-access and file-intake timers start and stop
on demand.

### What this PR does

Before this PR:

Three main-process services kept timers running for the whole app
lifetime, even with remote access never enabled:

- `RemoteAccessService`: a 5s advertisement refresh and a 1s
token/journal/connection sweep.
- `AttachmentPresenceService`: a 100ms change-flush/expiry loop.
- `FileIntakeService`: a 1s upload cleanup sweep.

After this PR:

- `RemoteAccessService` starts the advertisement refresh only while LAN
ingress is up. The sweep starts when ingress opens or a connection
arrives, and stops once ingress is closed, no connections remain, the
agent hub has no journals, and no attachment selections are still
presented (so device revocation still reaches them).
- `AttachmentPresenceService` replaces the 100ms loop with a one-shot
100ms coalesced broadcast after a change, plus a single timeout at the
earliest selection expiry.
- `FileIntakeService` starts its cleanup sweep only while uploads are
staged, and stops it once they drain.

With remote access unused, these services keep no timers.

Fixes # N/A

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- After ingress closes, the remote-access sweep keeps running until
journals drain and presented selections clear, so expiry and revocation
still work.
- `AttachmentPresenceService` uses plain `setTimeout`, cleared in a
registered disposable, because each timer is a one-shot that reschedules
itself.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Lengthening the intervals: the services still wake while idle, and
expiry/flush latency gets worse.

<!-- Template from
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md?-->
<!--  Thanks for sending a pull request!  Here are some tips for you:

https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
-->

### What this PR does

Before this PR:

With an AWS Bedrock provider and a Claude model, no prompt is ever
cached. `anthropicCacheFeature` writes
`providerOptions.anthropic.cacheControl`, but `@ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock`
(Converse) only reads `providerOptions.bedrock.cachePoint` on whole
messages, so every Bedrock request goes out with no cache point and pays
the full input price each turn.

After this PR:

A new `bedrockAnthropicCacheFeature` runs right after
`anthropicCacheFeature` for Claude models on Bedrock and puts a
message-level `bedrock.cachePoint` on each message that holds an
Anthropic marker (`ttl: '1h'` when the provider uses the one-hour
lifetime, except Claude Opus 4.1, which AWS lists as five-minute only).
Bedrock now writes the prefix on the first turn and reads it on the next
ones. Other Bedrock models are unchanged.

<!-- (optional, in `fixes #<issue number>(, fixes #<issue_number>, ...)`
format, will close the issue(s) when PR gets merged)*: -->

Fixes #23724

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Cache points go on whole messages only. `@ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock`
4.0.96 ignores them on content parts, and newer 4.x versions read both
levels, so setting both would double the count past Bedrock's limit of
four.
- Only Claude models get cache points. Bedrock rejects a cache point on
models without prompt caching ("You invoked an unsupported model or your
request did not allow prompt caching", seen live on Llama 3.3 70B,
Ministral 3 8B, Qwen3 32B and gpt-oss-20b, which the `aws-bedrock`
preset ships). Claude is detected with the existing
`stripBedrockDottedVendorPrefix` and `VENDOR_PATTERNS.anthropic`,
because `isAnthropicModel` does not match prefixed ids such as
`global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`.
- The step reads the same marker holders `clampCacheMarkers` counts, so
the existing four-breakpoint budget carries over.
- The tool-definition marker has no equivalent in the installed SDK, so
it is not converted. Tool definitions come before the system prompt in
Bedrock's cache prefix, so the system cache point still covers them.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Writing `bedrock.cachePoint` inside `anthropicCacheFeature`: it would
mix two wire formats in one transform. A separate feature follows the
existing `gatewayAnthropicCacheFeature` pattern.
- Including Amazon Nova: it accepts five-minute cache points but rejects
`ttl: "1h"` ("Extended TTL prompt caching is only supported for
Anthropic models"), so it is left for a separate change.

pending scroll after a file switch, `scrollToLine` on both editors) was
still there but nothing triggered it.

After this PR:

below the row, with a "N more matches" / "Show less" toggle.

note and scrolls once its content loads, in both the rich editor and

row and outside its click target, so clicking a match does not also

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Matches render as a variable-height block under the file row (as
Zettlr's global search does) rather than as child tree rows.
`DynamicVirtualList` already measures each item, so rows grow correctly.
- The display is restored as it was before (3 matches + toggle). Search
still computes up to 50 matches per file; showing all of them would make
the sidebar very long.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Deleting the unreachable locate/scroll code instead of restoring the
feature. Rejected: the removal was not mentioned in #16026, the search
service still computes per-line matches, and the badge alone does not
help users find the match.
- Matches as child rows of the file node (VS Code search view style).
This gives fixed row heights and keyboard navigation between matches,
but `FileTree` nodes are `file | folder` and only folders can have
children, so it would need a third node kind excluded from rename,

fix(media): revoke private channel attachment reads (#9077)

## Summary

Removed private-channel members can currently download attachments if
they know the URL. With `BUZZ_MEDIA_READ_MODE=enforce`, fresh GET, HEAD
and Range requests check current membership and readable references on
the primary database. Removed members receive 404; remaining members
retain access, and rejoining restores access. Thumbnail aliases use the
parent attachment’s permissions.

Publication checks also prevent copied private URLs from granting new
access. They cover attachments, link previews, profile pictures,
banners, group pictures and emoji. Persona creation and changed-avatar
edits, plus team and individual snapshot imports, transfer animated
posters and animations under the agent’s signer before profile
publication. Failed persona transfers preserve existing local records;
import failures appear in the results.

Authorization uses bounded queries, a two-second statement deadline and
transaction-local JIT suppression. An index on edit targets avoids broad
scans. Publications have a 512-reference limit, and capacity waits up to
500 ms before refusal.

Protection defaults off. Existing downloaded bytes cannot be recalled.
All modes stop creating immutable HTTP cache entries.

### Related issue

Related approaches: #7565, #5185, #8451 and #8444. This change evaluates
live stored references directly.

### Testing

Published head: `3d1aa7431cc495a001a0f13e95e2e422c5a77ab1`, rebased on
main `2cd40badb85de059a6916206e133da7a0a88fb2e`. Push hooks were
**SKIPPED** with explicit author approval. Current-head HTTP, full
package, PostgreSQL migration/media and profile-filter mutation checks
are pending; CI is pending. The earlier complete HTTP journey passed at
`f20b449262` (identical source tree), with its evidence attributed
separately. Earlier failing preview/report-fixture runs are preserved;
they do not count as passes.

The HTTP journey covers upload/publication, fresh GET/HEAD/Range
revocation and rejoin, emoji replacement, edited previews, persona
visibility and non-reference decoys. The migration regression forces an
index timeout, verifies no 0086 history or media tables, then proves a
migrator through the base's 0085 can restart.

Human attachment removal/rejoin testing passed on the pinned
`1f08a8e0fd2edf19dc94321f7258518149fe1bf6` trial. Native animated
persona edits and team/individual import acceptance remain incomplete.
That old-snapshot database stays intact and cannot run the reconciled
binary; a new trial needs a separate fresh database.

### Rollout prerequisites

- Build and verify the reference index before shadow mode. Small
databases can auto-migrate through one atomic 0086 migration within the
configured timeouts. It builds the index before creating the media
tables, so failure records no new migration version. Large deployments
must disable auto-migration and prebuild indexes concurrently.
- **Enforce remains blocked unless the operator can rule out SDK/CLI
attachment edits and the unverified agent-harness edit producer.**
SDK/CLI edits still omit attachment metadata. That behavior is deferred,
not fixed. Removing this blocker requires latest-effective attachment
metadata across successive edits, no restoration of removed files, and
an upload → successive edits → GET/HEAD regression.
- Validate client signer compatibility and split emoji publications
above 512 references before enforce mode.
- Complete the human workflows above in an isolated community with
enforce enabled.
- Follow the [index deployment
guide](https://github.com/block/buzz/blob/honor/private-channel-media/docs/private-media-index-deployment.md)
and [operator
guidance](https://github.com/block/buzz/blob/honor/private-channel-media/docs/operator-private-media.md)
for rollout and rollback.

The [prebuild timeout
finding](https://github.com/block/buzz/pull/9077#discussion_r4486221478)
and [avatar-transfer
finding](https://github.com/block/buzz/pull/9077#discussion_r4486221458)
are implemented and independently reviewed.

### Schema change checklist

- [x] Additive expand and code deployment; no backfill or contract
phase. Prebuild/verify before shadow under either schema deployment
path.
- [x] No SQL function, trigger, procedure, rule or foreign key added.
Signed events are untouched.
- [x] No migration mutates existing rows.
- [x] Migration and desired-state schema match. Catalog parity, target
parsing, future partition inheritance and upgrade refusal are covered.
- [x] Old/new binaries coexist for serving. Suspend community deletion
during expansion and while rolled back to a binary with the old deletion
catalog.
- [x] Keep auto-migration disabled on old binaries after schema
expansion; sqlx rejects unknown versions.
- [x] Migration lock timeout 1 s; statement timeout 5 s. Small populated
databases build inline within those budgets; large deployments use
concurrent child-index prebuild/attachment with auto-migration off.
Missing, invalid or wrong indexes fail verification.

Manage community NIP-FI policy with enable, disable and status (#9176)

## Summary

Operators can enable, disable and inspect a community's stored NIP-FI
requirement through signed POST/GET
`/operator/communities/nip-fi-policy` and `buzz-admin nip-fi-policy`.
This replaces the old enable-only endpoint and drops the
`nip-fi-upgrade` command added earlier in this PR, along with obsolete
compatibility code.

Each saved intent binds its desired state and observed generation/state.
Every accepted new intent advances the generation, including same-state
changes. Committed retries recover history without reapplying policy;
stale requests are refused. Current status exposes one pair of reusable
`expected_*` preconditions. Historical receipts remain readable after
policy changes or target deletion, including old rows with null
preconditions. Their UUIDs cannot be reused for new requests.

Migration 0085 stays additive; main’s default-channel recovery migration
retains version 0084. It preserves old receipt rows and INSERT
compatibility. Operator instructions cover use, recovery and client
migration: [usage
guide](https://github.com/block/buzz/blob/33a1c0bb87a6fa10212eb4ec60788e24189627e2/docs/operator-nip-fi-upgrade.md),
[client
contract](https://github.com/block/buzz/blob/33a1c0bb87a6fa10212eb4ec60788e24189627e2/docs/operator-nip-fi-policy-client.md).

### Rollout and containment

The old `/operator/communities/nip-fi-upgrade` route is removed; GET and
POST return 404 without its old auth handler. A pending sponsorship
client still targets that route. Migrate that client to the supported
API and deploy it with mutation dispatch paused before this relay
version reaches its fleet. Its complete CAS preconditions must be
durably saved before first dispatch and reused unchanged after a crash
or lost response. This is a pending integration dependency, not a claim
that the caller is deployed.

Close `BUZZ_NIP_FI_UPGRADES_ENABLED` on every old relay. Keep
`BUZZ_NIP_FI_CHANGES=false` on new relays. Apply schema first and finish
the whole-fleet rollout before opening the new gate and resuming
migrated clients. Before opening the new gate, verify the deployed
artifact SHA on every pod and probe each pod directly: the old route
must return 404, and a fresh, well-formed, signed policy request with a
new UUID must return 503 `upgrades_disabled`. A committed retry is not a
gate probe. Old pods with the old gate open can still accept unfenced
enables. Do not roll back to those writers after a policy operation. The
old variable is no longer read by this version; the new gate defaults
off and controls both directions.

Read accepted intent in `receipt`, current preconditions/effective
policy through status, and effective discovery through `/info`. Enable
stays `pending` because receipts cannot certify fleet-wide socket
closure. Under global `enforce`, stored disable leaves FI effectively
required. Closing the gate preserves receipt recovery; use a fresh CAS
disable or existing archive controls for containment. Preserve uncertain
requests and their UUIDs. This PR performs no live state change or
deployment.

N/A

Published repair head: `33a1c0bb87a6fa10212eb4ec60788e24189627e2`,
incorporating main `39d5159caf`. The Git policy guards now apply only to
matched paths. Unknown GET/POST paths on relays without a web directory

[buzz] Recover interrupted default-channel auto-joins (#9045)

**Bug**

Default channels are channels that new community members should join
automatically. If the database could not list those channels—for
example, because its connection pool was busy—an invite claim or an
in-app admin add still admitted the member to the community. That member
could then remain outside the default channels permanently.

**Cause**

Community admission was saved before channel joins started. If listing
the channels failed, the relay logged the error and stopped. Retrying
the invite or admin add did not help: the member already existed, so the
relay skipped the joins.

**Fix**

Save a marker for unfinished channel joins in the same database
transaction as admission. If listing or joining channels fails, keep
that marker. Retry when the member next authenticates, claims the invite
again, or is added again by an admin. One channel's failure does not
stop attempts to join the others.

Retries preserve the existing membership rules:

- A member who leaves a channel during recovery stays out of it.
- Work from an earlier admission cannot add channels or clear pending
work after the member is removed and admitted again. Each admission has
a unique marker, checked under a database lock.
- A reconnect still checks whether the member allows the original admin
to add them to channels.
- Once recovery finishes, later connections do not enroll the member in
newly designated default channels. The operator command `buzz-admin
add-member` continues to add community membership only.

**Limits and rollout risks**

Recovery needs one of those later requests; there is no background retry
timer. This change does not repair members missed before it was
installed.

Channel announcements and notifications keep their existing best-effort
behavior. A failure after channel membership is saved can still lose an
announcement; this change does not replay it.

Migration 0084 adds an optional UUID column to `relay_members`. Apply it
before running the new code. Older relays ignore the column. The
migration has a five-second lock timeout, so it fails rather than
waiting indefinitely for its table lock. It adds no triggers, functions,
procedures, rules, foreign keys, or data backfill.

fix(db): keep retained fence proofs when a probe fails (#9200)

## Summary

A failed replica fence probe no longer drops the proofs already
retained, so one failed probe no longer sends every read to the writer.

**Why.** `run_probe` called `fence.close()` on any probe error, which
cleared the ring. Until the next successful probe 500 ms later,
`fence.newest()` was `None` and every routed read went to the writer
with `reason="uninitialized"`. Under load this showed up as a steady
share of `bridge_query` reads labelled `uninitialized` on every pod,
while `heartbeat_age` stayed small. The module already documents that a
retained entry's proof never decays: a failed probe proves nothing new,
but it doesn't make an earlier proof wrong. So clearing the ring only
cost reader capacity.

**What changes.** A failed probe logs and records nothing. The retained
entries stand. A probe that keeps failing still closes the fence through
the existing 30 s staleness gate (`FENCE_STALENESS`), and
`heartbeat_age` remains the liveness signal. Regression handling is
unchanged: an epoch change or a same-epoch token regression still clears
the ring in `record()`. `close()` has no production caller left and
becomes a test hook.

**Likely trigger.** The masked-activity check
(`ProbeError::MaskedActivity`) counts a client backend whose state is
`active` with a `NULL` `xact_start` as masked. A backend that has just
started a statement can briefly show as `active` before its `xact_start`
is set, so busy writers hit this transiently. Under pgbench on Postgres
17, between 0.3% and 1.3% of scans saw such a backend. This PR doesn't
change that classification. See the debt below.

No protocol, schema, metric or client change.

### Testing

- `replica_fence::postgres_tests::failed_probe_keeps_retained_proofs`
(new, no database needed, so it runs in the unit lane like its
neighbours): records an entry, runs a probe tick against a closed writer
pool (the probe fails), then asserts `newest()` and `resolve()` still
return the entry, and that a rewound token recorded under the same epoch
after the outage is a `TokenRegression`. Mutation-checked on Blox:
putting `fence.close()` back on the error path fails it, including when
only the regression assertion is left.
- On Blox: the full `buzz-db` Postgres lane, the `buzz-db` unit tests,
`cargo fmt`, clippy for `buzz-db` and `buzz-relay`, and a `buzz-relay`
build.

### Rollout

There's no flag. Rollback is a revert. After deploy, watch:

- `buzz_db_route_decision{decision="writer",reason="uninitialized"}`
should drop to about 0 once a pod has booted, and the
`decision="reader"` share should rise.
- `buzz_db_replica_heartbeat_age_seconds` should stay small. Staleness
is now the only thing that closes the fence on probe failure, so this is
the liveness signal.
- `reason="stale"` may rise a little. `newest()` returns `None` for an
empty ring and for one older than the staleness gate, and both are
labelled `uninitialized`. Bounded reads can also miss the budget for one
tick when a probe beat is missed and fall back as `stale`. Some of
today's `uninitialized` share is expected to move to `stale` rather than
disappear.

## What got simpler

`ReplicaFence::close()` leaves the production API. A probe error now has
one effect (log and keep proving from what's retained) instead of a
second path that discards valid state. The probe loop is split into a
one-tick function that the test calls directly.

Identified, out of scope:
- `buzz_db` warnings, including this probe's failure warning, are
dropped by the relay's default log filter (`buzz_relay=info`), so
operators can't see why a probe fails.
- `MaskedActivity` misclassifies the transient
`active`-without-`xact_start` state. Treating it as not-open looks
sound, because such a backend's transaction starts after the scan, but
it touches the proof and deserves its own review.
- The probe's exclusive advisory lock waits behind channel writers'
shared locks, so a slow writer delays the probe.
- Probe failures have no metric. With retained proofs a failed probe no
longer shows up as `uninitialized` routes, and its warning is filtered
out of the logs (above), so intermittent failures are now invisible. A
probe-failure counter would fix that.
- An epoch rotation that fails still leaves an opening for a restore
that keeps the epoch. `TokenRegression` clears the ring, so if the
rotation `UPDATE` then errors, the next sample stores the rewound token
under the old epoch against an empty ring. This PR doesn't change that
path. A writer-side high-water token kept outside the ring would close
it.
- `newest()` gives the same `uninitialized` label to an empty ring and a
stale one, which hides a dead probe in route metrics.

perf(loadgen): spread seed writes across channel creators (#9206)

## What

`buzz-loadgen seed` signed every channel create, member add, and thread
root with the community owner. In private channels without human
members, the owner also signed all the history. The relay limits HTTP
calls per pubkey (default 300 a minute), so a community with thousands
of channels can't be seeded against a relay that keeps its default
limits. The seeder doesn't retry a 429, so the seed fails partway, and a
torn-down `run_id` can't be reused.

Take one community with 20,000 private channels: the owner alone signs
more than 40,000 writes, which is over two hours of its quota. Human
authors had the same problem on a smaller scale. A human in hundreds of
consecutive private channels signed hundreds of history posts within
seconds.

Now the community owner creates its first 8 channels, and each further
block of 8 gets its own creator identity (`Role::Creator`, derived from
`run_id`). A creator signs its channels' kind:9007 and kind:9000 events
and their thread roots, and `run` looks roots up by the creator. That
keeps every creator well under one minute of quota, whatever the
community's channel count.

History and replies still rotate across humans: a private channel's own
human members, or its creator when it has none. Because only humans look
roots up, the creator signs nothing but roots in their channels. No
amount of history or replies can push a root out of `run`'s newest-100
lookup.

Human signers can still bunch up, for example a human in hundreds of
consecutive channels or a deep thread. To cover that, a seed write the
relay throttles now waits out the `retry in <n>s` window the relay names
and tries again, up to 10 times, before it counts as failed.

Compatibility: a community with up to 8 channels is seeded as before,
apart from the retries. An existing fixture with that shape keeps
working with `run`, including its root lookups.

## What got simpler

Nothing got simpler. This adds a creator role and a retry loop, which is
the smallest change that makes large fixtures seedable against default
limits.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p buzz-test-client --all-targets
-D warnings`, and `cargo test -p buzz-test-client --lib loadgen`, run on
a Linux workstation at the head commit.
-
`no_channel_creator_signs_more_seed_writes_than_one_minute_of_its_quota`
seeds a private community of 400 channels against a fake relay. The
community has wide channels, a tier of humans in 280 channels each, and
runs at 2x. The test requires every creator to sign fewer than 300
writes. With the owner signing everything, it fails: the owner signs all
7,212 writes.
-
`throttled_writes_wait_out_the_quota_and_a_lasting_quota_fails_the_seed`:
when every write gets two 429s it is retried and the seed passes. When
the quota never clears, each write is tried 11 times and the seed fails
with the quota error.
- `private_channels_add_every_member_before_anything_is_posted` now uses
20 channels. It checks that every create, member add and root is signed
by its channel's creator, that the owner keeps channels 0–7, and that
every other post is by a human member.
- `root_lookups_search_the_channel_creators_posts` checks that `run`
searches for roots by the owner in a community's first block and by the
block's creator after it, across two communities.

feat(relay): runtime-tunable history-read and AUTH concurrency caps via feature flags (#9170)

## Goal

Give operators a way to relieve database pressure in seconds, without
restarting relay pods. Today every concurrency limit is an environment
variable, so changing one means a rollout. During an incident, that
rollout's restart sets off a reconnect storm of its own.

## What changes

**Two runtime-tunable caps.** Each is read from an integer feature flag
in a new process-wide evaluation context, and re-read every 5 s:

| Flag | Caps | Ceiling |
|---|---|---|
| `buzz.relay.concurrency.history-reads` | subscription-history reads
holding a reader connection (the #9132 gate) | the existing `pool −
pool/5` share, which keeps readers free for authorization |
| `buzz.relay.concurrency.auth` | verified NIP-42 AUTH frames running
their database checks | none (unbounded today) |

- **Flags can only tighten.** A positive value is clamped to the
ceiling. Zero, a negative value, no value, or a provider that never
initialized leaves the gate at its ceiling, which is today's behavior.
Once LaunchDarkly has delivered values, they stay in force through a
later outage, so a cap tightened during an incident survives a provider
blip.
- **Lowering never cancels admitted work.** A lowered gate admits
nothing new until the work in flight falls under the new limit.
- **Visibility:** `buzz_concurrency_limit{gate}` reports the applied
limit (`0` means no limit), and each change logs a line.

**One resizable gate.** `HistoryReadGate` becomes
`buzz_db::ConcurrencyGate`, a FIFO semaphore whose limit can move
anywhere in `1..=ceiling`:
- Lowering it forgets free permits and records any shortfall as debt.
- A permit released while there is debt is retired instead of returned.
- Raising it repays debt first, then adds permits.

All of this, and admission itself, settles against the debt under one
lock, so a newer limit always supersedes an older one; there is no
background resize task to race. Tokio hands a released permit to a
queued waiter before it runs; if that waiter is then cancelled, tokio
returns the permit to the semaphore directly, so admission retires any
permit it gets while debt is outstanding. The AUTH cap uses the same
type.

**AUTH shedding.** The permit is taken after signature verification, so
only real logins queue for the database checks. The wait is bounded at 2
s. A shed login gets a bare close with no `OK`, exactly like an auth
timeout. I chose this from what each client does on main today:
- **`OK false`:** the desktop app retries on an unjittered 60 s ladder.
Mobile parks the session until the app resumes. The agent harness fails
at startup.
- **Bare close:** the desktop app, mobile, the agent harness and the CLI
all reconnect on their jittered, capped backoff.

On the relay, the shed is visible as access line
`denied/concurrency_limit` and as
`buzz_auth_outcomes_total{outcome="concurrency_limit"}`.

**The feature-flag provider is chosen at startup.**
`BUZZ_FEATURE_FLAGS_PROVIDER` takes `static` (the default),
`environment` or `launchdarkly`, with `BUZZ_LAUNCHDARKLY_SDK_KEY` and an
optional `BUZZ_LAUNCHDARKLY_RELAY_PROXY_URL`:
- **Exactly one provider.** The value is parsed into a single provider,
so there is no stacking and no fallback, and the evaluator never changes
for the life of the process. The variable sits outside the
`BUZZ_FEATURE_FLAG_` namespace, so it can never be read as a flag.
- **Startup failures.** Local misconfiguration fails startup: an unknown
provider, a missing key, or a malformed proxy URL. LaunchDarkly being
unreachable, or rejecting the key, does not. The relay starts on
declared defaults, the SDK keeps connecting, and
`buzz_feature_flags_ready{provider}` shows whether the provider has
initialized. A revoked key must not crash-loop every pod over a tuning
knob.
- **Every build carries the LaunchDarkly adapter.** It stays inert
unless selected, so one published image serves every deployment and each
deployment's configuration pins its provider.

## Design-doc amendments (`crates/buzz-feature-flags/README.md`)

- **Provider selection.** The compile-time "exactly one provider"
contract becomes the startup selection above. The only-one guarantee now
holds per process instead of per build.
- **Startup.** Failing closed now covers local configuration only.
- **Guardrails.** "Flags may choose between equivalent implementations
only" gains one exception: a flag may set an operational limit as long
as it can only tighten it, and shedding under that limit stays
retryable.
- **Evaluation context.** `EvaluationContext::for_process()` adds a
process context, which LaunchDarkly sees as a single `relay`-kind
context keyed `relay`.

## What got simpler

- **Removed the compile-time provider contract:** the nested fixture
crate (with its own 2.8k-line `Cargo.lock`), its 229-line contract test,
and the exact-one `compile_error!` guards it required consumers to copy.
One startup parse plus a unit test replaces them.
- **One gate type serves both caps.** The history-read gate became that
generic type instead of gaining a sibling.
- **Net change:** about −2.3k lines.

## Review-Proven Rules applied

- **#1:** shedding is retryable (`PoolTimedOut` → CLOSED for history, a
bare close for AUTH) and never an empty success. Provider failures are
logged and surfaced through a gauge.
- **#2:** the gate settles every limit change and permit release under
one lock. The table test covers lowering while idle, lowering below the
count held, lowering then raising before holders leave, lowering then
raising past the count held, and restoring the ceiling.
- **#3:** the tests drive the production call sites:
`Db::get_channel_window_with_session` under a lowered and raised cap
(Postgres), and `handle_auth` under a full AUTH gate. The controller
test runs the real refresh loop.
- **#4:** values are clamped, waits are bounded, and the refresh runs on
a fixed interval with skipped missed ticks.
- **#9:** AUTH shedding sends clients down their jittered reconnect
backoff rather than an unjittered or terminal path (see above).

## Review rework (`92a975c8`, `3f09cb33`)

- **Keys renamed** to `buzz.relay.concurrency.*`: LaunchDarkly keys
cannot be renamed later, and the flag project may be shared with other
services.
- **Shutdown:** LaunchDarkly's final flush has no deadline of its own,
so `close()` now runs it on a detached thread and waits at most 2 s,
after the audit drain. (The blocking pool would not bound it: the
runtime waits for blocking tasks when it drops.)
- **Refresh loop:** a panicking refresh is caught, logged and counted
(`buzz_concurrency_limit_refresh_panics_total`), and the next tick
retries, so the caps cannot freeze silently.
- **Runbook:** `docs/operator-concurrency-caps.md`, covering how to
tighten a cap and the cases in which a tightened cap returns to its
ceiling (mistyped or deleted flag, pod started during a provider
outage).
- **AUTH test:** asserts the second login passes the gate and returns
its permit; the gate permit is renamed so it no longer shares a name
with the NIP-FI effect permit.

Gated on a Linux workstation at `92a975c8` (`3f09cb33` is rustfmt only;
`cargo fmt --check` passes there): clippy `-D warnings`,
`buzz-feature-flags` (50), `buzz-relay --lib --bins` (1740), the new
modules under parallel `cargo test`, and the Postgres AUTH tests (27).
Each new test fails under its mutant: the refresh without
`catch_unwind`, `close()` with no deadline (hangs until killed), and the
AUTH handler with the gate skipped.

workstation:

- `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo clippy -p buzz-feature-flags -p buzz-db -p
buzz-relay --all-targets --all-features -D warnings`.
- `buzz-feature-flags` with and without `launchdarkly` (50 and 24

fix(relay): route live REQ events by each filter's own channel scope (#8519)

🤖
## Summary

**The problem.** A Buzz client that watches one channel's details (its
name, topic, members) gets them once and then never hears about changes.
If someone renames the channel, the client keeps showing the old name
until it reloads. A related problem: when a client watches a channel's
messages and something community-wide in the same request, the channel's
new messages stop arriving.

**The fix.** The relay (the Buzz server) now decides where to send new
events separately for each part of a request, instead of once for the
whole request.

### Background: how a client watches for events

A client sends the relay a **subscription**: a request made of one or
more **filters**. Each filter describes some events, for example
"messages in channel X" or "the details of channel X". The relay answers
in two phases:

1. **History.** It sends the stored events that match, then a marker
that says "history is done".
2. **Live.** It keeps the subscription open and pushes each new matching
event as it arrives.

For the live phase, the relay must decide which new events a
subscription may receive. It sorts new events into **topics**: one topic
per channel, plus one community-wide topic for events that belong to no
channel. A subscription only hears the topics it signed up for. This is
the security boundary that keeps a private channel's events away from
people who cannot read it.

### Why it broke

The relay picked the topics **once for the whole subscription**, with
one rule: if every filter names its channels with an `#h` tag, listen to
those channels; otherwise, listen only to the community-wide topic.

That rule fails in two cases:

- **Channel details.** A channel's details are a special event (kind
39000) that the relay signs and stores under the channel itself. Clients
ask for it with a `#d` tag, not `#h`: `{kinds:[39000], "#d":[X]}`.
Because the filter has no `#h`, the rule chose the community-wide topic,
which never carries channel X's events. The client got the current
details in history, and then no updates. (NOSTR.md documented this gap
as a future enhancement.)
- **Mixed requests.** If a request had one filter for channel X's
messages and a second filter with no channel, the rule chose
community-wide for both. The channel filter silently lost its live
messages.

### What changes

Each filter now gets its own topics:

| Filter | Live events it receives |
|---|---|
| Names channels with `#h` | New events in the channels it names and may
read |
| Channel details (kinds 39000–39003) that name channels with `#d` |
Updates for the channels it names and may read, plus community-wide
events |
| Names no channel | Community-wide events, the same as before |

The relay then sends a new event only through a filter that **both**
matches the event **and** listens to that event's channel.

### Why this is safe

- **No filter can see more than it already could.** A filter's channels
come only from the channels it names, and each one must pass the same
read-permission check the history phase uses. A private channel's
outsider gets neither history nor updates (tested).
- **One filter cannot widen another.** This is the reason for per-filter
topics. The simple fix, "add the `#d` channels to the whole
subscription", would leak. Some channels, such as system channels and
future channel types, appear only to a filter that names them. With one
shared set of topics, a sibling filter such as "all channel details
created by person P" (`#P`) would start to receive live updates for such
a channel, even though that channel never appears in its history. #8469
closed this leak for the history phase. This PR keeps the live phase
consistent with it (tested).
- **Requests that worked before behave the same.** A request whose
filters all name `#h` channels got the union of their channels before.
Each filter's own `#h` condition already rejected the other filters'
channels, so per-filter topics deliver exactly the same events. A filter
with no channel keeps the community-wide topic, as before.
- **Recent joins are not missed.** Each server caches who may read which
channel for a few seconds, so a server can briefly miss a new member.
When a request names channels the cache does not list, the relay checks
them against the database. Before, it did this only when every filter
used `#h`. It now checks every channel any filter names, including `#d`.
This matters more now, because a live scope is fixed when the
subscription starts: a missed channel would stay missing until the
client subscribes again. The check keeps the same token restrictions
(tested). More than 2048 `#h` channels is still refused. More than 2048
named channels in total because of `#d` is not refused: the `#d` names
then skip this check and live routing, so the request gets history from
the cached access set and community-wide live updates, as before this
PR. The legacy desktop app sends one unbatched `#d` query for every
channel the user is in (tested).
- **Clean up stays exact.** A subscription signs up for each topic once,
even when several filters name the same channel. It releases each topic
once on close, on replacement with the same ID, or when access to a
channel is revoked. Revoking one channel removes only that channel; the
subscription keeps its other channels and its community-wide topic. The
tests check the counts on each path.

### Not in scope

A filter that reaches a channel without naming it still gets that
channel's events in history but not live. This is unchanged: before this
PR, such filters listened only to the community-wide topic too. Examples
are a channel-less filter, which history fills with every channel the
reader can see, and the "all system channels" opt-in (`#t:["system"]` or
`#P`).

### Related issue
Follow-up to #8469.

### Testing
- Two new Postgres tests drive the real request handler. (1) A
channel-details subscription receives updates after history, from this
server and through the handler that receives other servers' events from
Redis. (The test calls that handler directly. It does not cover
publishing or Redis transport.) A private channel's outsider receives
nothing. (2) In a mixed request, the channel filter and the channel-less
filter each keep their live events, and a sibling filter by creator
(`#P`) or system label (`#t`) does not receive a channel it did not
name.
- A Postgres test with a stale access cache: a just-joined channel still
reaches both a `#d` filter and an `#h` filter beside a channel-less one,
in history and live.
- New unit tests cover the per-filter topic rule and the subscription
registry.

fix(relay): deliver multi-node fan-out concurrently and never drop silently (#9195)

## Problem

Each relay node runs one consumer for events that other nodes publish to
Redis. It delivered them one at a time and awaited the access gate
(visibility and membership lookups) for each event. Under load it fell
more than 4,096 events behind the pub/sub broadcast. Each `Lagged(n)`
then skipped `n` events for good: nothing replayed them, and plain
subscribers were never told.

In a 15-node load test, about 50% of cross-node events were skipped at
10x load and about 75% at 13x. Throughput at 13x was also *lower* than
at 10x. Loadgen didn't show this, because it only times events that
arrive.

## Change

- **Concurrent delivery.** A dispatcher reads the broadcast and only
routes. It drops local echoes and queues each event on one of 16 workers
by `(community, topic)`. Each worker delivers its queue in order, so a
channel's events keep their order while different channels deliver
concurrently. `handlers/multinode_fanout.rs`
- **Known loss closes the affected connections.** An event is lost when
its worker's bounded queue (1,024 events) is full, or when it isn't
delivered within 2 s of this node reading it from Redis, whether it
waited in the broadcast, behind a backlog, or in a stalled delivery.
`ChannelEvent` now carries `received_at`, stamped by the pub/sub
subscriber. For a lost event, the relay sends `CLOSED "resync: live
delivery lagged"` to every sync the event would have reached (NIP-AR
Sync rule 5). It also closes every connection the event would have
reached, so those clients reconnect and catch up from their cursor.
Matching runs before the access gate, so a recipient that would have
been filtered out may be closed too. That costs a reconnect, never a
leak.
- **A lost ephemeral event is only counted.** Presence, typing and
observer frames are never stored, so no reconnect can replay them.
Losing one fences and closes nothing; it is still never delivered past
its deadline. Without this, one stale global presence event would close
nearly every mobile connection in the community, since every mobile
client subscribes to presence.
- **Unknown loss closes every subscribed connection.** If the dispatcher
itself lags the broadcast, it can't know which events it skipped. It
resyncs every sync (unchanged) and closes every connection that has a
subscription.
- **Immediate fence.** Each affected connection is fenced as soon as the
loss is detected. The live fan-out send path (`send_to_text_bytes`,
local and cross-node) delivers it nothing from then on. The fence is
written under the connection map's write guard, and the send path checks
it and queues its frame under one read guard, so no frame slips in
between the check and the send.
- **Why 2 s.** The mobile client resumes from the newest `created_at` it
received, minus 5 s of slack. The desktop app (block/buzz-app) resumes
960 s before its connection last heard the relay, which already covers
the full 900 s `created_at` drift. While an event waits, local fan-out
and other workers keep moving that cursor. The fence stops the cursor,
and the deadline means no withheld event is more than 2 s older than the
fence, so a reconnect replays it. Without the deadline, an event stuck
behind a long backlog could be withheld past the slack and never
replayed.
- **Paced closes.** Only the close is delayed. One closer task closes at
most 50 connections per 10 ms (5,000/s per node). A drop in a hot
channel therefore can't become a reconnect storm (Review-Proven Rule 9).
- `fan_out_pubsub_event` is now split into `take_local_echo` and
`deliver_pubsub_event`, so the dispatcher can check echoes before
queueing. Its behavior is unchanged.
- **Limits (mobile):** replay works while the 2 s deadline, plus the
writer's clock skew and its publish delay, stays under the client's 5 s
slack. The relay accepts `created_at` up to 15 min off, so a writer
clock more than about 3 s slow can still put an event behind the cursor.
An ordinary reconnect has the same limit today; closing it needs a
client rewind instruction, which is out of scope here. The desktop app's
960 s resume window has no such gap. A dispatcher that falls behind
without overflowing the broadcast still never delivers a late event, but
it detects the loss, and fences, late. Events skipped by dispatcher lag
are never seen. Neither case is bounded by the deadline, which is a
cutoff for attempting delivery, not a guaranteed fence time.
- **What a load-test rerun should watch:** under sustained overload the
deadline turns backlog into steady closes (up to 5,000/s per node), and
reconnecting clients replay from the same database pool. Watch
`buzz_multinode_fanout_dropped_total{reason="stale"}`,
`buzz_multinode_fanout_lag_closed_total` and the reconnect REQ rate next
to pool wait. On dispatcher lag, the dispatcher scans the subscription
registry and fences each subscribed connection synchronously, so also
watch how long it stays behind after a `Lagged`.

Metrics:
- `buzz_multinode_fanout_lag_total` (dispatcher lag) and
`buzz_multinode_fanout_total` (delivered) keep their meaning.
- `buzz_multinode_fanout_dropped_total{reason}` counts lost events:
`queue_full`, or `stale` for one not delivered by its deadline. A lost
ephemeral event counts as `ephemeral` instead and closes nothing.
- `buzz_multinode_fanout_lag_closed_total` counts close attempts for a
loss, one batch at a time.

## Rollout

- Staging first. The load-test rerun at 1x, 10x and 13x happens after
merge, with the staging load tests planned once the current relay
changes land. At 1x, expect zero `dropped_total` for stored kinds and
zero `lag_closed_total`. Report delivered %, `dropped_total{reason}`,
`lag_closed_total`, reconnect REQ rate and pool wait.
- Then one production cluster before the rest.
- **Rollback trigger:** `lag_closed_total` climbing steadily, or
reconnect REQs pushing pool wait up, at normal load. Rollback is a plain
revert and redeploy: there are no schema, config or wire changes.

## Ordering

Order is kept within a `(community, topic)`. Events on different topics,
for example a channel event and a global event, can now reach one
subscriber in either order. Before this change they arrived in Redis
arrival order. Nothing in the relay depends on order across topics: the
access gate re-reads membership and visibility per event. Clients order
by `created_at`.

## What got simpler / known debt

- The fan-out loop in `main.rs` shrinks to one `spawn` call, and the lag
handling lives next to the delivery code.
- No new config knobs. The worker count and queue size are constants
until a load test shows they need tuning.
- **Known debt, not in this PR:** a Redis pub/sub reconnect can still
lose events silently for plain subscribers. Syncs are already resynced
in that case (`artifact_sync::watch_link`), but ordinary subscriptions
are not.

## Tests

`handlers::multinode_fanout::tests`, each checked with a mutant on Blox:
- events reach their subscriber through the workers, in publish order
- a full worker queue closes exactly the dropped event's recipients
- a lost ephemeral event (full queue or stale) is counted as `ephemeral`
and neither fences nor closes, while a stored event lost on the same
queue still closes
- a local echo on a full queue closes nothing
- dispatcher lag closes every subscribed connection
- after a known loss or dispatcher lag, a recipient gets no newer live
event while it waits to be closed
- the fence also withholds relay-local fan-out
- an event that waited out its deadline before dispatch is lost, never
delivered
- an event behind a backlog is delivered inside its deadline, and past
it is lost (its recipient fenced and queued for close), never delivered
late (paused clock)
- a delivery that stalls on a database that never answers is cut off at
the deadline and handled as lost
- the closer cancels in paced batches (paused clock), and counts each
batch as it closes

perf(db): bound since-limited events reads with the month-floor literal (#9197)

## Summary

A newest-first `events` read whose own `since` is at or above the
recent-pass floor now runs as a single recent pass. Postgres prunes it
to the recent monthlies at plan time instead of locking every partition.
Results are unchanged.

**Why.** `split_for` skipped any read whose `since` was at or above the
floor (`since_prunes`), on the theory that its `since` already prunes.
It does, but only as a bind parameter. Once a prepared statement
switches to a cached generic plan, Postgres prunes bind-parameter bounds
at execution, after `AcquireExecutorLocks` has already locked every
`events` partition and its indexes. Live REQs with a recent `since` are
this shape, for example `#p` mention reads from reconnecting agents.
Under load they spill past the 16 fast-path lock slots and contend on
`LWLock:LockManager`. The ceiling PR (#9157) named this gap as
identified debt.

**What changes.** Such a read now gets the same `Split` as other recent
reads, so the recent pass carries the floor literal (plus the ceiling
literal for regular-kind reads) on `e.created_at` and on
`m.event_created_at` for `#p`. `Split` gains `older: bool`. It is false
when the read's own `since` is at or above the floor, because no row
below the floor can match, so no older pass follows a short recent pass.
A read whose `until` falls below the floor stays unsplit, as before.

No protocol, schema, index or client change.

### Related issue

Follow-up to #9157 (its identified debt: bind-parameter `since` reads).

### Testing

- `recent_pass::tests::split_eligibility`: the table now records not
split / ceiled / open and whether an older pass follows. New rows:
`since` at the floor, a recent `since` with regular, any and
addressable-only kinds, and a recent `since` with `until` below the
floor.
- `recent_pass::tests` in-memory exactness: adds a `since`-at-floor
split that runs exactly one pass and returns the rows at or above the
floor.
-
`postgres_tests::since_bounded_mention_read_locks_only_recent_partitions`
(new): runs partition maintenance, inserts `#p` rows at the floor, now,
one second below the ceiling and one day below the floor, then reads
with `since = floor`. The production path returns the three recent rows
through the mention join. Under `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan`
the recent pass locks only the partitions holding those rows. The
unsplit read locks every partition.
- The partition-lock helper from #9157's test is now shared by both lock
tests.
- Diagnostic on Postgres 17.11 with the 19-partition layout partition
maintenance keeps, for a `#p` read with `since` at the floor (not
committed):

| | `events` partitions locked | Relation locks | Non-fast-path locks |
  |---|---|---|---|
| Before (bind-only `since`, generic plan after five runs) | 19 | 26 |
10 |
  | After (floor and ceiling literals) | 2 | 9 | 0 |

`EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)` before appends all 19 partitions. After, it
appends only the previous and current monthlies.

Mutation-checked on Blox. Each of these fails the new Postgres test or
the unit tests: removing the `since_prunes` split, ignoring `older`, and
dropping the `e.` literal.

## What got simpler

Nothing got simpler. The change adds one flag to the existing `Split`
type and no new concept. The duplicated partition-lock reader in the
#9157 test became one shared helper.

Follow-ups to the CLI's Buzz desktop credential support, for a person

perf(relay): serve restriction rows for 10 s with cross-pod invalidation (#9199)

## Summary

The restriction cache (`AppState::restriction_state_cached`) is the
relay's hottest auth read. With a 1 s max age, most per-request
ban/timeout checks miss and hit Postgres. This change serves cached rows
for **10 s** and makes every restriction write invalidate them on every
pod, so the longer age only bounds a pod that misses the notification.
That's the same bound the membership cache already uses.

### What changes

- **`RESTRICTION_CACHE_MAX_AGE` goes from 1 s to 10 s.**
- **Cross-pod invalidation for every restriction writer.**
`AppState::invalidate_restrictions(tenant)` drops the community's rows
locally and publishes a new `CacheInvalidation::Restrictions` over the
existing Redis cache-invalidation channel. The writers that call it:
- kind 9040 ban, 9041 unban, 9042 timeout, 9043 untimeout
(`moderation_commands.rs`)
- admin HTTP `DELETE /members/{pubkey}/ban` and `/timeout`, which
invalidated nothing before
- report-resolution and direct ban/timeout, at the enforcement
convergence point so crash recovery repeats it. Timeout invalidated
nothing before.
- recording an agent's owner (HTTP token/NIP-OA owner link and both
invite claims, through `disconnect_unowned_agent_clusterwide`). The
agent's cached row predates the link and lacks the owner's restriction;
the old disconnect-path drop used to cover this.

Before this change, unban, timeout and untimeout cleared only the
handling pod, and bans cleared other pods only through the disconnect
path.
- **Community-wide drop.** An agent's row also carries its owner's
restriction (`restriction_state` reads `users.agent_owner_pubkey`), and
the cache can't tell which agents a target owns. Dropping the
community's rows covers owner→agent without a lookup. Restriction writes
are rare next to the reads the cache absorbs.
- **Stale-refill fence.** Before, a read in flight when a ban landed
could refill the old "allowed" row. The 1 s age bounded that; at 10 s it
needs a fence. The restriction cache now uses the epoch-fenced fill the
community-active cache already had: a fill is published only if no
invalidation happened since its read began.

### What got simpler

- That shared-read, epoch-fence and max-age logic is now one generic
`FencedCache<K, V>` (`fenced_cache.rs`). `CommunityActiveCache` becomes
a type alias over it.
- The restriction cache drops its hand-rolled fill in `state.rs`, plus
`CachedRestriction` and the separate `restriction_reads` gate.
- `disconnect_pubkey_local` no longer touches the restriction cache, so
roster removal and self-leave stop flushing it.

Net +146 lines, tests included (new writer assertions plus the generic
cache tests, moved from `community_active.rs`).

### Accepted bounds

- A pod that misses the Redis notification (subscriber reconnect window,
or an older pod mid-rollout) serves a stale row for at most 10 s. Older
pods log and skip the unknown `op`. Bans still close sockets clusterwide
through conn-control, and socket admission and moderation-command actors
still read fresh.
- `banned` is computed at read time, so an expiring ban can outlast its
expiry by up to 10 s. That fails closed. Timeouts still lift on time,
because the cached row carries `muted_until`.
- An owner link drops the whole community's rows, not just the agent's,
because the cross-pod message is community-scoped. A link happens once
per agent, so the extra refills are negligible.

### Identified debt (not in this PR)

- `open_channels_cache` and `HostCache` hand-roll similar read_at/epoch
logic. `open_channels_cache` could move onto `FencedCache`.
- Concurrent waiters whose shared read *fails* each re-read on their own
(`SharedReads::turn`). Sharing the failure is a separate change.

## Test plan

- `fenced_cache` unit tests cover:
  - concurrent misses sharing one read
  - entries served inside the max age and expired past it
  - invalidation fencing an in-flight fill and its waiters
- scoped invalidation dropping only matching keys while also fencing
fills
  - errors not being cached
- `state::tests::restriction_invalidation_drops_the_community_rows`
checks that local and received drops remove the target's and an owned
agent's rows, and that another community's rows stay.
- `owner_link_drops_the_agents_cached_restriction_row`: a timed-out
owner's fresh agent, admitted over HTTP with that owner, is refused its
first write. Removing the owner-link invalidation fails it.
- Postgres tests now assert that the cached row is dropped by:
- kinds 9040–9043
(`restriction_commands_drop_the_cached_restriction_row`)
  - admin HTTP unban and untimeout, with other-community isolation
  - direct ban and timeout through the enforcement convergence point
- Mutants (epoch check, scoped epoch bump, `Restrictions` arm, admin
unban invalidate, convergence invalidate, 9040 invalidate) each fail
their test.
- `stored_writes_honor_cached_ban_until_it_ages_out` pins the 10 s bound
with literal ages: a 9 s old cached ban still refuses a write, and a 10
s old one is reread. Raising `RESTRICTION_CACHE_MAX_AGE` to 11 s fails
it.
- On a cloud workstation: fmt, file-size, clippy (`buzz-pubsub`,
`buzz-relay`), the nextest unit suites, and the full `buzz-relay`
Postgres lane. In the full lane, 622/626 passed. The other 4 are tests
this change doesn't touch, and each passes in isolation at both the base
commit and this head.
- Two relays sharing one Postgres and Redis: a timeout, untimeout and
admin-HTTP lift on one relay take effect on the other's next write, a
few ms after the first relay acknowledges.

Pin sqlx to the upstream fix for a cancelled BEGIN (#9192)

## Problem

sqlx 0.9.0 counts a transaction only after Postgres acknowledges its
`BEGIN`. If the future is dropped while `BEGIN` is still in flight (a
cancelled REQ history read, a client that disconnects, a timeout), sqlx
doesn't queue a `ROLLBACK`. The pool's release ping then reads the late
`BEGIN` reply, and the writer pool hands the connection to the next
borrower while it is still inside that transaction. The reader pool
already closes such connections in its release check
(`Db::read_pool_options`). The writer pool has no release check.

Load tests showed what happens next:

- `there is already a transaction in progress` (25001) on the next event
read's `BEGIN`.
- Sometimes a burst of `current transaction is aborted` (25P02). The
leftover from the event read is `READ ONLY`, so the next write fails and
aborts it, and every later statement on that connection fails until the
connection is closed. During a burst, ban checks failed closed with 503
and window reads returned 500.
- A read-write leftover would also leave autocommit writes uncommitted,
and the next read's `ROLLBACK` would discard them.

## Change

- Pin every sqlx crate to transact-rs/sqlx#4394 (merged, not yet
released). That commit takes the transaction count before the `BEGIN`
round trip, so a cancelled begin queues its `ROLLBACK`. The crates share
types, so they have to move together. The pin also picks up the other 23
commits between v0.9.0 and that fix, including the libsqlite3-sys fix
`sqlx-sqlite` was already pinned for.
- Add a regression test,
`writer_pool_postgres_tests::begin_cancelled_in_flight_leaves_no_writer_transaction_open`.
It holds `BEGIN` in flight behind a paused proxy and times it out, for
both the event read's `BEGIN ... READ ONLY` and a plain `begin()`. It
then asserts that the next borrower's autocommit write commits and that
its backend is `idle`, not inside a transaction.

Other upstream changes in the pin that reach the Postgres path:
`TCP_NODELAY` on sockets (transact-rs/sqlx#4336), reuse of the TLS
connector across connection attempts (transact-rs/sqlx#4242), a fix for
a memory leak when the statement cache is disabled
(transact-rs/sqlx#4337), a describe-time generic-plan change used only
by the macros (transact-rs/sqlx#4286), and the `whoami` default-user fix
(transact-rs/sqlx#4303). The rest are SQLite, MySQL, CLI, or docs
changes.

Remove the pin once sqlx 0.9.1 ships.

## What got simpler

The lockfile loses its second `sqlx-core` copy, which the
sqlx-sqlite-only pin used to pull in. No runtime code changes. A
pool-level release check would have fixed the same bug, but it costs a
round trip on every writer release.

Comments that described the 0.9.0 behavior as current are refreshed: the
reader pool's release check (`Db::read_pool_options`) and the lease
heartbeat (`EntityDeletionStore::heartbeat`). The reader test
`proof_timeout_mid_begin_leaves_no_reader_transaction_open` asserted
that the release check closed the connection left mid-`BEGIN`. With the
pin, sqlx rolls that transaction back itself, so the test now asserts
the check finds nothing to close. That also catches a sqlx regression
the check would otherwise hide.

Identified debt (not in this PR): the release check's open-transaction
arm, and the reader-session `default_transaction_isolation` pin it
depends on, are now only a backstop against a sqlx regression. They
could be removed in a follow-up.

## Testing

- Against sqlx 0.9.0 (main's `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` at 962b3fdd), the
new writer test fails for each `BEGIN` form on its own. The event read
fails with `cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction`, and after
a plain `begin()` the next borrower's backend is not `idle`. With the
pin it passes 5/5.

feat(cli): manage sidebar sections with `buzz sidebar sections` (#9191)

Replaces #8759, which had its head on a fork. This branch also carries
the stars/mutes (#8781) and sort mode (#8784) work that merged into it.

## Summary

Sidebar sections were desktop-only. They live in the encrypted
kind:30078 `channel-sections` preference, and the CLI had no command for
it. An agent that mirrors a team's Slack channels into Buzz could create
the channels but not group them into sections.

This adds `buzz sidebar sections`:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `list` | `{sections: [{id, name, icon?, order}], assignments:
{channel_id: section_id}}` |
| `create --name <n> [--icon <emoji>]` | Adds a section at the end;
returns `section_id` |
| `update --section <s> [--name] [--icon \| --clear-icon]` | Renames a
section or changes its icon |
| `delete --section <s>` | Deletes a section; its channels go back to
the default list |
| `reorder --section <s>...` | Sets the section order; unlisted sections
keep their order after the listed ones |
| `move --channel <uuid>... --section <s>` | Moves one or more channels
into a section |
| `unassign --channel <uuid>...` | Returns channels to the default list
|

`--section` takes a section id, or a section name when the name is
unique. One `create` and one `move` per section set up a whole sidebar:

```bash
buzz sidebar sections create --name "Engineering" --icon "🛠"
buzz sidebar sections move --section "Engineering" --channel <uuid> --channel <uuid>
```

## Design

- **Wire compatibility.** `sidebar_doc.rs` ports desktop's per-field LWW
register document (`channelSectionsSync.ts`, `sidebarLwwMap.ts`,
`sidebarLaneStore.ts`): decode, shape validation, projection, encode,
and `setRegs` stamping (`v = max(now, newest + 1)`, one shared stamp per
edit, unchanged leaves not rewritten). CLI writes merge with desktop
edits field by field. The CLI also imports the flat (meta-less) format
that mobile writes.
- **One user action is one publish.** Each command reads the head once
and publishes once. A multi-channel `move` therefore lands as one event.
A command that changes nothing publishes nothing and prints `"message":
"unchanged"`.
- **Never overwrite what it cannot read.** If the head fails decryption,
signature verification, or decoding (for example, an unknown `meta.v`),
`list` and every write fail. They do not treat the head as empty. A
write that the relay reports as dominated exits 5 (`Conflict`).
- **Same limits as desktop.** 100 sections, 1,000 assignments, and the
65,535-byte ciphertext cap. Channel IDs are stored in lowercase
hyphenated form, which is the form desktop matches.
- **No relay change.** The relay already stores `channel-sections` as a
generic replaceable kind:30078 event.

## Scope notes

- The commands always edit the **signing identity's own** sidebar,
because the document is NIP-44 encrypted to self. A local agent that
runs with the user's key (for example, `BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY` set to the
user's nsec) sets up that user's sidebar. A managed agent with its own
key edits only its own sidebar.
- The request also mentioned "an equivalent agent/MCP tool". Agents use
`buzz-cli` for agent-facing operations, so the CLI help and
`crates/buzz-cli/README.md` document the `list` output contract. This PR
adds no separate MCP tool. This PR does not change `desktop/`
(deprecated; see #8840).
- `create` does not dedupe by name, which matches desktop. If a setup
script runs twice, it creates duplicate sections, and later `--section
<name>` lookups then fail as ambiguous. They do not pick one silently.

## Testing

- `cargo test -p buzz-cli`: 513 pass. The sidebar tests are:
- A journey through the production command functions against a fake
relay. The fake relay checks the head filter (`kinds`, `authors`, `#d`,
`limit`). The journey covers list, create, a multi-channel move as one
publish, a no-op repeat, invalid input with no publish, reorder, update,
unassign, delete, and the decrypted event's kind, tags, and document
shape.
- Rows for head selection (newest `created_at`, lower id on a tie,
another author's event ignored), `created_at = head + 1` after a
future-dated head, a mobile flat head, an unreadable head, a tampered
head, the count limit, the ciphertext cap, the NIP-44 plaintext cap, an
empty `--icon`, and a dominated write (exit 5).
- Each guard was mutation-checked: removing it makes at least one test
fail.
- **Desktop interop:** a CLI-written document was fed to desktop's own
`decodeDoc` and `projectSections` (from
`desktop/src/features/sidebar/lib`, run with node). Desktop decoded it
as a meta document, its projection matched the CLI's exactly, and
`canonical(json) === canonical(encodeDoc(tree))`. So desktop treats the
head as settled and does not republish it.
- **Live read:** `buzz sidebar sections list` against a real relay
correctly decrypted and projected a desktop-written sidebar (2 sections,
2 assignments). I ran no live writes.
- `cargo clippy -p buzz-cli --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo fmt
--check` are clean.
- An agent review ran. It reported no blockers, and its optional
findings were fixed: tests now bind the relay filter and head selection,
a silently dropped head is an error, a no-op `reorder` writes nothing,
the `safe_int` overflow is fixed, channel IDs are canonical, and an
empty `--icon` is rejected.

### Manual test steps

1. `cargo build -p buzz-cli`, then set `BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY` (your nsec)
and `BUZZ_RELAY_URL`.
2. `buzz sidebar sections list`: you see your current desktop sections.
3. `buzz sidebar sections create --name "CLI test" --icon "🧪"`: within a
few seconds, a "CLI test" section appears at the bottom of the desktop
sidebar.
4. `buzz sidebar sections move --section "CLI test" --channel <uuid>
--channel <uuid>`: both channels move under "CLI test" in desktop.
5. In desktop, rename the section. Then run `buzz sidebar sections
list`, which shows the new name.
6. `buzz sidebar sections delete --section <id>`: the section
disappears, and its channels return to the Channels list.

The author ran these steps and confirmed the result on an earlier head.

**Live re-test on this head** (rebased on `main` at 7fe3e6f), with the
Buzz Desktop credential provider against the production relay:

- `list` read the existing desktop-written sidebar (2 sections, 9
assignments).
- `create` (with an icon), `move`, a repeated `move` (published nothing;
`"unchanged"`), `update --name`, `list`, `unassign`, and `delete` were
all accepted.
- After cleanup, `list` output was byte-for-byte equal to the snapshot
taken before the test.

**`buzz-app` Desktop interop:** Buzz Desktop now ships from
`block/buzz-app`, so I checked the CLI document against its code at
`main` as well. `projectSidebarRecord` and `projectSidebarPreferences`
(`src/features/relay/`) project the CLI document to the same sections,
and the projected record equals the CLI document, so Desktop does not
republish it. The document also satisfies the Desktop signer rules in
`src-tauri/src/identity.rs` (`version: 1`, meta keys `v`/`s`/`a`,
section fields `name`/`icon`/`live`/`order`, 16-hex device ids).

Note: Desktop loads `channel-sections` by fetch, not by live
subscription, so a CLI edit shows in an open Desktop on its next sidebar
refresh (for example, a restart), not instantly. This is the same for
edits from another device.
