Chat UI: let the floating monitor settle after the viewport restore before dragging it (#16909)

## Summary

`Chat UI Tests (chat)` keeps failing on unrelated PRs in the floating
monitor geometry step:

```
[ui] resize landed at 260x141 with limits {'minWidth': 256, 'maxWidth': 260, ..., 'inline': 'opacity: 1; left: 988px; top: 0px; ... max-width: 260px; ...'}
AssertionError: [ui] FAIL: resize width: expected 296, got 260
```

Seen on the staging runs for #16890 and #16782 today, with identical
numbers. The limits logging added in #16885 is what shows the cause, and
it is not the stale viewport limit #16861 and #16885 assumed.

`use-floating-panel-layout.ts` sets `maxWidth = constraints.width -
left`. With the 1280 px viewport and 16 px insets the constraint box is
1248 px wide, and `1248 - 988 = 260`. So during the resize the panel was
moved to the right edge, though the step had just dragged it to the top
left and the limits wait before the resize saw room for 296 px.

The sequence:

1. The active drag into the shrunken viewport's corner snaps the panel
back to its anchor, so its horizontal position is "right edge"
(`intent.left === null`).
2. At the 260 px viewport that anchor puts it at left 0. On
`set_viewport_size(viewport)` the next layout pass moves it back to the
right edge, but left 0 is inside the restored viewport too, so
`wait_for_box("viewport restore", is_inside)` can pass before that pass
runs.
3. `drag_monitor_to(0, 0)` then grabs a panel still at left 0 and drops
it at left 0. `finishDrag` only makes an axis absolute when the drag
changed it ("a null axis stays anchored to the far edge"), so the
horizontal anchor stays on the right edge.
4. The native resize fires the layout's `ResizeObserver`,
`placeAxis(null, maxLeft)` puts the panel at the right edge (left 988),
and the width is capped at the 260 px left there.

The component is doing what it is designed to do: a user cannot start a
drag in the frame between a window resize and the layout pass. Only the
test grabs it too early.

## Change

`tests/studio/playwright_chat_ui.py`, test only. After restoring the
viewport, wait for the monitor to stop moving (`wait_for_settled`, the
frame-polled helper `pointer_drag` already uses) before the `is_inside`
check and the drag. The layout pass runs within that wait and restarts
it if it moves the panel, so the drag starts from the panel's real spot.
The comment on the limits wait from #16885 no longer blames a stale
viewport limit.

## Testing

- The failing runs' logged limits match the sequence above exactly
(`left: 988px`, `max-width: 260px`, `1248 - 988 = 260`), on two runs on
different staging repos.
- `python -m py_compile tests/studio/playwright_chat_ui.py`.
- This PR's own `Chat UI Tests (chat)` run exercises the step. The
failure is a timing race, so a single green run cannot prove the fix by
itself; I will keep watching the staging runs after it lands.

```
    torch.testing.assert_close(g, w, rtol = 1e-4, atol = 1e-6)
E   AssertionError: Tensor-likes are not close!
E   Mismatched elements: 1 / 32 (3.1%)
E   Greatest absolute difference: 3.814697265625e-06 at index (0, 6) (up to 1e-06 allowed)
```

Seen on the staging runs for #16109, #16886, #16882 and #16877 today
(`cpo-kwargs1`, `kwargs2`, `kwargs3`, `kwargs5`, `kwargs6`, always
`qwen3_lora`).

The cause is test pollution. #16793 added
`test_load_probe_memo.py::test_fastmodel_adapter_load_probes_base_config_once`,
which runs `FastModel.from_pretrained` up to the weights. That load does
what it does in real use: it swaps PEFT's LoRA forwards
(`peft.tuners.lora.layer.Linear` and 8 other LoRA layer classes) for

Neither side's product code is wrong. #16793's loader change and its

Tests only.

imported during the load falls back to the `_unsloth_original_forward`
the wrapper carries.

`test_matches_trl[...-qwen3_lora]` pins stock PEFT forwards for its
duration (through `monkeypatch`), since its reference is TRL on stock
PEFT. This keeps it deterministic whatever else ran earlier in the
worker.

Studio: fill the H3 conditioner's pinned arenas once, before registering (33% faster cold pin) (#16887)

## Summary

MiniMax-H3's quantized conditioner is pinned eagerly at load
(`pin_module_in_place`, video_minimax_h3_te.py): its weights are copied
from the safetensors mmap into pinned host arenas. Profiling an 8 GB pin
showed the copy itself is the smaller part. Most of the time is arena
allocation: `registered_pinned_empty` zero-fills every byte of a fresh
buffer (to fault its pages) and only then are the weights copied in, so
every arena byte is written twice.

This PR fills each arena once:

- Arena placement (largest first, first fit, 512-byte alignment,
power-of-two arena sizes) is computed up front, unchanged.
- Each arena is then filled by `_fill_arena`: the tensor copies plus
zeroed gaps and tail, on an 8-thread pool, before it is registered. The
copy faults the pages, so the separate zero pass is gone. Every arena
byte has the same value as before.
- `registered_pinned_empty(nbytes, fill=None)` takes an optional `fill`
that runs instead of `zero_()`, before `cudaHostRegister`. Other callers
are unchanged. The torch pinned-allocator fallback fills after
allocating.
- Owners are replaced only after every copy succeeded, so a failed copy
now leaves the module untouched (before, some owners could already be
replaced). The caller still falls back to streaming unpinned.
- `_parameters` / `_buffers` are still replaced rather than `.data`, so
the mmap is still released after the pin.

## Evidence

Synthetic 8.6 GB safetensors file (Gemma-3-27B-shaped int8 weights plus
bf16 tensors), loaded via mmap into a module; each arm runs its own
tree's code through the real registered-arena path; 4 repeats per arm,
interleaved; cold runs evict the file with `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)`.
Colab A100-SXM4-40GB VM, 3 vCPU, 83 GB RAM, torch 2.14.1. Median
(range):

| | base | base A/A | head | head A/A |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| hot page cache | 3.795 s (3.78-4.32) | 3.772 s (3.74-3.79) | 3.402 s
(3.39-3.41) | 3.402 s (3.38-3.47) |
| cold page cache | 6.052 s (6.01-6.23) | 6.050 s (6.03-6.08) | 4.070 s
(4.01-4.12) | 4.022 s (3.99-4.13) |

About 10% faster hot and 33% faster cold, both well outside the A/A
spread. Running the pin from a worker thread gives the same numbers. An
earlier L4 run of the same change gave the same ratios (3.53 vs 3.99 s
hot, 4.20 vs 6.24 s cold). Every arm passed a bitwise and `is_pinned`
check against a fresh reload of the file.

Measured and not adopted: `MADV_POPULATE_READ` on the source (slower),
`MAP_POPULATE` (slower), `MADV_HUGEPAGE` on the arena (no effect), and
`preadv` straight into the arena (faster cold, but it would read the
file's bytes rather than memory's).

## Tests

- `test_h3_low_vram_stream.py`: copies run on the pool with the same
placement and byte-identical arenas as a 1-thread run, owners and tied
tensors preserved; a failed pooled copy replaces nothing.
- `test_diffusion_registered_slabs.py`: the arena contents at register
time equal the final contents and only unused bytes are zeroed; `fill`
errors propagate.
- The four new tests fail on base and pass on head. H3, registered-slab,
integrated-GPU, segment and pin-arena suites: 1092 passed; 7 tests fail
identically on base and head (3 `test_diffusion_h3_trainer`
regional-compile cases, 2 `test_diffusion_segment`, 2
`test_integrated_gpu_no_host_pin`) and are unrelated.

## Not proven

- The 7 s vs 29 s run-to-run swing seen on a G4 with the real
conditioner was not reproduced: repeat spread here was 1-3%. Its cause
(memory pressure, a concurrent denoiser slab pin) is still open; this PR
removes a full write pass but does not claim to remove that variance.
- Only 3-vCPU Colab VMs were used, not a G4 or a many-core host, and not
the real 27 GB conditioner in a full Studio load. Linear scaling
suggests roughly 1.3 s hot and 6.6 s cold saved for 27 GB, which is an
extrapolation.

Studio: prequant fingerprint check on a thread pool, zero-copy (13x faster first load verify) (#16879)

## Summary

The first load of a new prequantized diffusion checkpoint runs a
one-time integrity check: it md5s every quantized weight and compares
against the fingerprint recorded at build time
(`_verify_packed_fingerprint`). On a G4 this took 23 s for MiniMax-H3
NVFP4 (313 weights, md5-canonical-v2), most of the first-load time. The
check hashed one weight at a time on one thread, and copied every
weight's bytes twice before hashing (tensor to numpy to `bytes`, then
`head + payload`).

This PR keeps the check exactly as strong (every weight, same digests,
same marker cache) and makes it cheaper:

- Hash a zero-copy `uint8` view of each payload (`memoryview` of the
numpy view) instead of `tobytes()` plus concatenation. The md5 input
bytes are identical, so recorded fingerprints still match.
- Hash weights on a thread pool (8 threads by default, capped at
`os.cpu_count()`). `hashlib.md5` releases the GIL for large buffers, so
this scales with cores.
- Both `canonical_weight_fingerprint` (md5-canonical-v2) and the older
`packed_weight_fingerprint` (md5-packed-v1) go through one shared
helper, `_digest_weights`, so both keep the same key order, skip
semantics and "a raise counts as uncovered" behaviour.
- `UNSLOTH_PREQUANT_FINGERPRINT_THREADS` overrides the pool size (`1` =
serial).

Nothing about what is verified changes: mismatch still falls back to
dense, the per-file "verified" marker keyed on path, size, mtime and
recorded fingerprint is untouched, and `sample` / `off` modes behave as
before.

## Evidence

Base = `origin/main` b75a4cd721, head = this branch. Each arm imports
its own tree in a fresh process (asserted), same model and seed, 5 timed
repeats, A/A arms in the same run.

64 torchao int8 5120x5120 Linears (1.68 GB of quantized weights), CPU,
`canonical_weight_fingerprint`:

| arm | median | min | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| base | 4.143 s | 4.097 | 4.276 |
| base (A/A) | 4.002 s | 3.904 | 4.106 |
| head | 0.321 s | 0.312 | 0.325 |
| head (A/A) | 0.309 s | 0.299 | 0.331 |

About 13x, far outside the A/A spread. All 64 digests are identical
across the four arms. At that rate the 11.5 GB H3 NVFP4 check goes from
about 23 s to about 2 s on a host with 8 or more free cores.

## Tests

- New `studio/backend/tests/test_prequant_fingerprint_threads.py`:
threaded equals serial for v2 and v1, the work runs on the pool, the
zero-copy digest equals md5 over `_canonical_bytes`, and the thread
count env parsing. On base 6 of 7 fail (the pool and env do not exist);
on head 7 of 7 pass.
- Prequant suites (`test_diffusion_prequant.py`,
`test_build_prequant_checkpoint.py`, `test_diffusion_fp8_prequant.py`,
`test_diffusion_segment_quant.py`, `test_prequant_legacy_int8.py`,
`test_prequant_native.py`, `test_prequant_safetensors.py`,
`test_diffusion_prequant_cache.py`, `test_video_prequant.py`,
`test_h3_prequant_mapped_read.py`, and others): 323 passed, 19 skipped
on both trees.

## Not proven

- FP8 and NVFP4 digests were not built here: torchao needs sm89+ /
Blackwell to construct them and no such card was available for this run.
The changed code is format-agnostic (the same bytes reach md5), and the
recorded-digest tests pass.
- The end-to-end G4 first-load time was not re-measured; the 2 s figure
is projected from the CPU hashing rate.

Studio LTX-2.5: read the hosted int8 checkpoint as native Linears when the DiT is offloaded (#16886)

## Summary

When a GPU is too small to hold the LTX-2.5 DiT, the int8 load offloads
it. Offload hooks cannot move torchao weights, so these loads skip the
hosted `LTX-2.5-INT8-ConvRot.safetensors` and quantize at load instead.
Concretely, an offloaded int8 load:
- stages the 36 GB of dense bf16 `transformer/` shards;
- quantizes 480 Linears into native (torchao-free) int8 at load;
- writes the 23.4 GiB result to the local prequant cache in the
background, while the first clip renders.

The hosted file already holds per-row int8 codes and float32 scales of
the same ConvRot-rotated weights. That is exactly what
`NativeWeightOnlyLinear` stores. This PR reads the hosted file directly
into native Linears whenever the plan offloads and the native W8A8
ConvRot build would run:
- no dense shards are staged;
- nothing is quantized at load;
- nothing is written to the cache.

## What / why / evidence

**What**
- **New `diffusion_native_hosted.py`:** reads the hosted int8 file into
native Linears. It refuses the file, and the load falls back to the
dense shards and the runtime build as before, unless all of the
following hold:
- the metadata (scheme, family, component, dtype, ConvRot kind and
group, min_features, excluded layers) matches the native build;
  - the quantized layer set equals the set the runtime build would swap;
  - the rotated layers are exactly those whose width the group divides;
  - zero points are all zero and there are no static activation scales;
- the recorded md5-canonical-v2 fingerprint verifies. This is the same
check the torchao load runs, through a plain-tensor `HostedInt8Parts`
view whose digests equal the `Int8Tensor`'s.
- **Planner (`video.py`):** when the artifact-sized plan still offloads
and the request resolves to int8 on a CUDA card with the W8A8 ConvRot
path, the planner stages the hosted file instead of the dense shards.
This applies to both the load's pre-download and the download panel's
plan.
- **Load (`video.py`):** after a native-cache miss, the load reads the
hosted file. A local native-cache hit still wins, so an existing user
replays the build they already have.
- **Scope:** opt-in per family (`native_offload_from_hosted_int8`, set
for LTX-2.5 only). `UNSLOTH_VIDEO_NATIVE_HOSTED=0` restores the old
path.

**Why.** The Nov 5 G4 16 GiB INT8 fresh first clip took 316.8 s. Its log
shows where the time went:
- `built 480 host linear(s) on cuda one at a time (25.8 GB in 100.8 s)`:
the dense shards were read from disk;
- a 94.8 s background cache write;
- a 99.7 s first encode alongside that write;
- a 58 s pin wait.

**Accuracy.** Frames are not bit-identical to base. The runtime build
quantizes the bf16 weights itself, while the hosted file was built by
the hosted-checkpoint builder. Both are per-row symmetric int8 of the
same ConvRot-rotated weights, but about 7-8% of codes differ by 1 and
the scales differ by about 0.6%. The codes this PR loads are the ones
Studio's resident int8 path (the default on cards that hold the DiT)
already uses. Measured against Studio's own bf16 render on the same VM:

| LPIPS (prompt v0 / v1) | vs Studio bf16 | vs Studio resident int8
(hosted file, torchao) |
|---|---|---|
| base (runtime native build) | 0.085 / 0.075 | 0.079 / 0.080 |
| head (hosted codes, native) | 0.097 / 0.047 | 0.086 / 0.054 |

Both arms of each tree are bit-identical to each other (A/A, PSNR 99
dB).

**Evidence. LTX-2.5 1280x704x121 two-stage distilled, INT8, held to a 16
GiB budget on a G4 (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell), Colab.** Base = main
b75a4cd721, head = this branch, one VM, one fresh process per arm.
- Page cache: every Studio arm first reads the pack, the hosted INT8
file AND the dense bf16 shards, so this table compares work, not disk.
- First clip = load + cold render.

| arm | load s | cold render s | first clip s | steady s / clip |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base fresh #1 | 16.8 | 85.1 (denoise 62.7) | 101.8 | 10.51 |
| base fresh #2 | 15.7 | 52.3 (denoise 34.3) | 68.0 | 10.60 |
| head fresh #1 | 34.8 | 40.5 (denoise 29.3) | 75.3 | 10.49 |
| head fresh #2 | 34.2 | 40.0 (denoise 29.2) | 74.2 | 10.49 |
| base returning | 18.5 | 149.8 (pin wait 85.9, encode 48.4) | 168.3 |
10.51 |
| head returning | 13.1 | 28.0 | 41.1 | 10.63 |

- **Base fresh varies a lot** (68 to 102 s) because its 23.4 GiB
background write (81 s) overlaps the first render. Head has no write.
- **Head fresh load** includes the one-time fingerprint verification of
the 24 GB file (about 20 s). A returning load reads the file in 0.6 s.
- **Base returning** reads its native cache file back, and pinning it
took 87 s from disk.
- **Disk:** head keeps 24 GB of hosted file instead of 36 GB of dense
shards plus a 23.4 GiB cache entry. A fresh user downloads 12 GB less.

**Same row with the dense shards on disk but not in the page cache**,
the condition of the Nov 5 row: the pack and the hosted file are
prewarmed, and the 35.4 GiB of `transformer/` shards are evicted before
every Studio arm. Same kind of VM, second session:

| arm | load s | cold render s | first clip s |
|---|---|---|---|
| base fresh #1 | 34.5 | 143.8 (pin wait 50.5, denoise 77.1) | 178.3 |
| base fresh #2 | 92.9 | 54.8 | 147.8 |
| head fresh #1 | 32.2 | 39.5 | 71.7 |
| head fresh #2 | 29.6 | 40.0 | 69.7 |
| base returning | 15.6 | 120.3 (pin wait 98.5) | 136.0 |
| head returning | 10.6 | 21.5 | 32.1 |

Head fresh is 2.1-2.6x faster and head returning 4.2x faster. Each
tree's two fresh arms render bit-identical frames, and the frames match
the first session's.

## Tests

New `studio/backend/tests/test_video_native_hosted.py` (11 tests, CPU,
tiny LTX2VideoTransformer3DModel written in the hosted layout):
- **Native layout:** the hosted file reads into exactly the runtime
native build's layer set, with the same `rot_group` / `act_int8` /
shapes. Codes and scales come from the file, and every dense tensor is
bit-equal to the dense model's.
- **Refusals:** wrong rotation group, other family, unrotated file,
different excludes, a missing layer, a static activation scale, and
corrupted codes (fingerprint mismatch) each fall back. So do a
weight-only or fp8 native build.
- **Fingerprint:** `HostedInt8Parts` gives the same canonical digest as
a torchao `Int8Tensor`.
- **Gating:** only an opted-in family with an int8, CUDA, W8A8 build
takes the hosted file, and the env switch turns it off.

These tests fail on main (the module does not exist).
`test_video_ltx25_prequant.py`, `test_video_prequant.py`,
`test_diffusion_prequant.py`, `test_diffusion_native_stream_build.py`
and `test_diffusion_native_quant.py` pass, except one test that fails on
main as well with this host's torchao 0.17
(`test_unpinned_torchao_host_copy_is_a_distinct_wrapper_over_the_same_data`).

## Not proven

- **Frames:** not bit-identical to base (different quantization of the
same weights, see Accuracy). Two prompts are not enough to call the
LPIPS difference either way.
- **Other hosts:** only the G4 at 16 GiB was measured. L4 / A100 offload
rows and a host with less RAM than the 24 GB file read were not run.
- **Compile:** no new compiled code. The modules are the same
`NativeWeightOnlyLinear` class the runtime build makes, so no compile
check was rerun on GPU.

Studio diffusion: overlap the quant scheme probe with the planner import on a cold image load (#16882)

## Summary

On a cold image load the load thread runs two slow serial steps back to
back: the planner's diffusers / transformers import (via
`_auto_keeps_bf16_reason`, about 6 s CPU) and then the quant scheme
probe, which spawns a child process and waits on it idle
(`_child_probe_table`, about 4-5 s on a cold card). This PR starts that
same child before the import, on a daemon thread, so the two overlap.

- `start_probe_table_prewarm` / `join_probe_table_prewarm` in
`diffusion_transformer_quant.py`; `_scheme_supported` consumes the early
table instead of spawning a second child.
- The early child only starts when the old code would have spawned one
(no in-process or persisted verdict for the card), under the same
`_CHILD_PROBE_LOCK`, and produces the same table, so the scheme decision
is unchanged.
- The load joins the child before anything reads free VRAM and before
the planner returns, so memory planning sees the same device state as
before (the child's CUDA context is gone).
- Logs `scheme probe ran beside the load` when it engages.
`UNSLOTH_DIFFUSION_PROBE_OVERLAP=0` restores the serial probe.

## Evidence

FLUX.2-klein-4B, one Colab L4 VM (12 vCPU, torch 2.13.0+cu130), base =
`origin/main` b75a4cd721, head = this branch, 3 repeats per arm, arm
order alternated per repeat. Fresh = new process, empty Studio home and
caches (weights already downloaded); returning = a second process.

| arm | load s (runs) | load + first image s (median) | steady s/img |
|---|---|---|---|
| base fresh | 30.4 / 28.89 / 28.56 | 50.1 | 2.08 |
| head fresh | 26.8 / 25.26 / 24.86 | 46.4 | 2.08 |
| base returning | 20.42 / 20.41 / 19.99 | 30.9 | 2.08 |
| head returning | 19.84 / 20.45 / 20.39 | 30.9 | 2.08 |

- Fresh load is 3.6 s faster (12.6%), load plus first image 3.7 s
faster. Head's slowest fresh load is below base's fastest; base fresh
spread is 0.33 s without the first cell on the VM.
- Returning loads are unchanged, as expected: the verdict is already
persisted, so no child is spawned.
- Steady state is unchanged.
- The engagement log line appears in all 3 head fresh runs (probe about
4.0-4.1 s) and in none of the returning runs.
- Every image is byte-identical across all 12 cells (one MD5 per
prompt).

## Tests

- New `studio/backend/tests/test_diffusion_probe_overlap.py` (5 tests):
the child starts before the import and overlaps it, the join happens
before free VRAM is read, the off switch, a cached verdict skips the
early child, an out-of-memory child result is not cached. All pass on
head; the overlap and ordering tests fail on base.
- Related backend suites: 887 passed, 8 skipped. A wider run of 89 load
/ planner test files: 9565 passed; the only failures
(`test_video_cosmos3.py`, 3 tests) fail identically on base.

## Not proven

- Studio's server already kicks this probe in the background at startup
when a diffusers model is in the local cache, so a user who waits after
startup may see no gain; the gain is for a load that arrives before that
warm-up finishes or a model not cached at startup.
- Only L4 with FLUX.2-klein-4B was measured: not G4, AMD, or other
models, and not cold-disk reads.
- If a family never reaches the probe on this load, the early child
costs up to about 4.5 s once; its result is persisted, so it is not paid
again.

Studio Qwen-Image-2.1: fused q/k RMSNorm + RoPE and broadcast modulation for eager renders on ROCm (#16891)

### Summary

A dense Qwen-Image-2.1 load is speed-deferred: images 1 and 2 (and image
3 while its background compile is pending) run eager, and the compiled
profile engages from the 3rd image. #15908 gave those eager renders a
fused q/k RMSNorm + RoPE Triton kernel and a broadcast decode-step
modulation, but kept ROCm on the stock diffusers step, because the
kernel relies on `libdevice.mul_rn` / `add_rn`, which the HIP libdevice
does not have.

On a Strix Halo (Radeon 8060S, gfx1151, torch 2.11.0+rocm7.13.0) the
stock eager step spends about 290 ms per denoise step on the elementwise
work #15908 removed on NVIDIA. This PR turns the same path on for ROCm:

- **Kernel on ROCm.** The products and sums the kernel must round
separately are plain Triton ops on ROCm, launched with
`enable_fp_fusion=False`, so nothing is contracted into an FMA. The
explicit `tl.fma` calls that mirror the card's complex multiply stay.
CUDA keeps the `*_rn` intrinsics and launches exactly as before.
- **`install()`** no longer refuses ROCm torch. The per-device
`probe_fusion` still decides the FMA pairing (gfx1151 probes `("x",
"x")`), and an unknown pairing or a JIT failure keeps the stock step, as
on NVIDIA.
- **Scope.** This is unchanged from #15908: only renders that a
speed-deferred load runs eager. Compiled renders, `speed_mode=off` and
the kill switch `UNSLOTH_DIFFUSION_Q21_EAGER_FAST=0` keep the stock
step. The Windows ROCm route runs speed tier `off`, so it is unaffected.

### Evidence

Everything below comes from one gfx1151 Linux job on one box (AMD CI,
exclusive GPU). The arms ran in the order base, head, base repeat, head
repeat. Base is main at the merge base and head is main + this change.
Each arm loads Qwen-Image-2.1 bf16 and renders 1024x1024 images at 25
steps with CFG 1, in this order:

- 1 warm-up image
- 4 new prompts
- one long render and one short (5-step) render of a prompt already seen

A forward wrapper times every denoiser call with device events, and
steps 12 of image 2 and of the long render ran under `torch.profiler`.

**Per decode step, device ms** (median of steps 2-25 of each image):

| image | base | base repeat | head | head repeat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (eager, warm-up) | 3978 | 3964 | 3693 | 3692 |
| 2 (eager, first new prompt) | 3982 | 3967 | 3701 | 3697 |
| 4-6 (compiled) | 3668-3679 | 3650-3656 | 3625-3634 | 3657-3659 |

- **Eager steps:** -7.1%, from 3964-3982 ms to 3692-3701 ms. The A/A
spread is 0.4% on base and 0.1% on head.
- **Compiled steps:** unchanged. Base and head overlap within the A/A
spread, and their images are bit-identical.

**Per image, wall seconds:**

| image | base | base repeat | head | head repeat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 104.8 | 103.9 | 95.2 | 95.8 |
| 2 | 110.8 | 102.3 | 95.3 | 95.4 |
| 3 (compile engages) | 115.0 | 105.9 | 107.4 | 105.8 |
| 4-6 (compiled) | 94.0-94.2 | 94.1-94.3 | 93.0-93.2 | 94.4-94.4 |

**Profile of one eager step** (image 2, step 12), per category in ms:

| kernels | base | head |
|---|---|---|
| GEMM | 2746 | 2745 |
| attention (AOTriton `attn_fwd`) | 524 | 522 |
| elementwise | 337 | 135 |
| copy / cast | 331 | 226 |
| norm (head: the fused kernel) | 19 | 53 |
| reduce | 23 | 0 |
| GPU busy | 3980 | 3681 |

**Kernel check on the device,** at the real decode shape (1, 4096, 32,
128) bf16:

- The fused kernel takes 0.49 ms per call; the stock RMSNorm + complex
RoPE pair takes 4.08 ms. There are 64 calls per step.
- 93 of 16.8M elements differ from the stock pair, each by one bf16 step
at its magnitude (max abs 0.031). The cause is the order of the fp32 sum
of squares. This is the same class of difference #15908 measured on
NVIDIA.

**Accuracy,** same prompt and seed:

- The eager image (image 2): head vs base LPIPS 0.0157, PSNR 31.1 dB.
- Compiled images 3-5 are bit-identical between head and base.
- Repeats are bit-identical within each side (base vs base repeat, head
vs head repeat).

**Engagement:** `diffusion.q21_eager: renders before the deferred
compile run the fused q/k RMSNorm + RoPE and broadcast modulation` is
logged on every head load and on no base load. On base, the kernel check
shows `install()` returning False on ROCm.

**NVIDIA:** the CUDA branch of `_kernel()` and the launch are unchanged,
and `_launch_options()` is empty there. I ran the same kernel check on a
Colab A100 against main's module and this branch's module, each in its
own process:

- Both install and engage.
- Both differ from the stock pair in 24 of 16.8M elements.
- Their fused outputs are byte-identical (same sha256 of the bf16
tensor).

### Tests

`tests/test_diffusion_qwenimage21_eager.py`:

`test_rocm_torch_takes_the_eager_step`. On ROCm torch the step now

Studio diffusion: settle device memory once per video plan, wake sd.cpp polls on server output (#16797)

Two fixed waits on the diffusion / video paths.

## 1. Video planner: settle device memory once per plan

For auto fp8 / int8 seeds, `_video_planned_auto_denoiser_scheme` asks
`_video_seed_stays_resident` twice in a row about the same card, and
each call ran its own `settled_snapshot_device_memory`, which sleeps up
to two 1 s intervals while free VRAM is below total minus max(2 GiB,
10%). That is always the case when the previous video pipeline is still
resident (the planner passes it in as reclaimable) or a chat model
shares the card. The planner runs both for `/video/download-plan` (which
the page awaits before loading) and inside the load itself.

The planner now settles once per call, lazily (only when a check
actually reaches the device read, so early exits still read nothing),
and passes that reading to both checks; each check adds its own
reclaimable credit to a copy of it. Same decision on one consistent
reading. On a 16 GiB card with 10 GiB free, a plan goes from 6 reads and
4 sleeps to 3 reads and 2 sleeps: up to 2 s saved per plan, and a load
plans twice (route, then load).

Decisions match a copy of the old planner across 36 cases (scheme x
requested quant x resident pipeline memory), each over 30 free / total
memory combinations; a settle that raises still returns `None`.

## 2. sd.cpp server: wake the job and readiness polls on server output

The sd-server job poll slept a fixed 0.4 s between status requests and
the readiness poll 0.5 s. The thread that drains the server's stdout now
sets an event for every line (and at end of output). The polls wait on
it and, after a line, check again after 20 ms with backoff (20, 40, 80,
160, 320 ms) before returning to the old interval, which stays the
fallback. Job status over HTTP is still the only thing that ends a job;
the server's own log line (`generate_image completed` in the pinned
build) comes just before the status flip, which is why a short burst
follows each line instead of a single check.

On a real loopback HTTP server with a piped stdout (5 runs each):

| | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| job status flip to return | 160 ms median (68 to 164) | 13 to 14 ms |
| bind to ready | 376 ms median | 16 to 17 ms |

That is up to 0.4 s per sd.cpp image or video job chunk and per server
load. Status requests stay bounded (at most about 50 per second while
lines stream, the old 2.5 per second when the server is silent, loopback
only). The pinned sd-server does not log HTTP requests, so the polls
cannot feed themselves.

## Tests

- New `tests/test_video_seed_settle_once.py` and
`tests/test_sd_cpp_server_log_wake.py` (42 tests): 17 fail with the old
code, all pass here.
- `tests/test_sd_cpp_*.py`, `tests/test_video_*.py`,
`tests/test_diffusion_*.py`: the same failing / erroring test IDs on
main and on this branch (pre-existing, unrelated), plus the 42 new
passes. An independent review found no race (a lost wakeup only falls
back to the old timer; the event is cleared after every wake, so it
cannot spin) and no change in deadlines, cancellation or progress order.

## Real sd-server A/B

Pinned sd-server (`master-982-0518b34-uaba3a1c`), SD 1.5 Q4_0,
`SdCppServer` from the merge base vs this branch, fresh process per arm,
interleaved base / head / head / base / base / head.

| | base | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T4 (CUDA, 512x512, 20 steps, 18 images per side): last server line to
`img_gen` return | 197 to 430 ms (about 330 ms typical) | 41 to 131 ms
(about 127 ms typical, includes the PNG encode before the status flip) |
| T4: load to ready | 0.54 to 1.07 s | 0.51 to 0.53 s |
| T4: sd-server's own `generate_image` time | 5.51 / 5.74 / 5.75 s |
5.84 / 5.69 / 5.71 s (same within run to run spread) |
| T4: status requests per image | 15 to 19 | 88 to 106 |
| CPU (256x256, 4 steps, 12 images per side): last line to return,
median | 264 ms | 54 ms |

The extra status requests (about 15 per second while a render streams
lines) do not slow the server's generation.

Also: the new tests pass on ubuntu-latest, macos-15 and windows-latest
(42/42 each). The readiness test now stamps the bind before it happens,
since a fast ready poll could return before the serving thread recorded
it under load.

## Not covered

- Avoiding the per-request LoRA copy when the LoRA and sd-server's
scratch dir are on different file systems was left out: it would change
how long staged files live.

transformers 5.23 renames gradient checkpointing to activation
checkpointing, and the Trainer now reads only the new names. On 5.23 the
reentrant setting Unsloth pins is lost, `use_gradient_checkpointing =

parallel check recognise `ActivationCheckpointingLayer`. Older
transformers releases behave as before.

Backend tests: importorskip the unsloth submodule a test uses, not the stubbable package (#16898)

## Summary

Since #16793 (`90e1e733c4`), Backend CI `(Python 3.13, g-r)` fails on
unrelated PRs. The last hour's staging runs for #16887, #16886 and
#16882 all show the same two tests:

```
tests/test_load_download_repos_mapper.py:11: in test_unmapped_lora_base_skips_the_remote_mapper
    from unsloth.models import loader_utils
E   ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'unsloth.models'; 'unsloth' is not a package
```

What #16793 tests (skipping the remote mapper for unknown LoRA bases) is
fine. The two new tests guard with `pytest.importorskip("unsloth")` and
then `from unsloth.models import ...`. In the backend job, several test
files stub `unsloth` at import time as a plain module
(`_stub_if_missing` in `test_audio_type_inconclusive.py` and others)
when the real package cannot be loaded. If one of those runs earlier in
the same xdist worker, `importorskip("unsloth")` returns the stub
instead of skipping, and the submodule import fails. Run alone, or in a
worker where nothing stubbed it, the tests pass. That is why it depends
on how the shard is laid out.

## Change

- `studio/backend/tests/test_load_download_repos_mapper.py`:
`importorskip` the submodules the tests use
(`unsloth.models.loader_utils`, `unsloth.models.loader`). With a stub in
place they now skip, the same as with no unsloth at all. With the real
package they run unchanged.
- `studio/backend/tests/test_backend_tests_stub_heavy_imports.py`:
`test_no_test_importorskips_bare_unsloth` fails if any backend test
calls `pytest.importorskip("unsloth")` on the bare package, and pins its
own detector both ways. No other backend test does this today. The rule
is narrowed to `unsloth`, since the `trl` stubs carry the attributes
their tests read.

## Testing

On `studio/backend`, with a one-line test file that stubs
`sys.modules["unsloth"]` as a plain module run first (what the shard
does):

| | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| stub first, then `test_load_download_repos_mapper.py` | 2 failed (the
error above) | 2 skipped |
| `test_load_download_repos_mapper.py` alone, real unsloth | 2 passed |
2 passed |
| `test_backend_tests_stub_heavy_imports.py` | 6 passed | 7 passed |

Report incomplete Studio streams in the CLI (#16868)

Fixes #16867.

When a Studio HTTP stream ends after a text delta, the CLI currently

Studio: start Blender MCP on mcp 2 (#16895)

Fixes https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/issues/16878

Enabling Blender MCP fails with "Could not connect to Blender MCP" since
Studio moved to mcp 2 (#16475). The pinned Blender MCP runtime imports
`mcp.server.fastmcp`, which mcp 2 removed (it was renamed to
`mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer`), so the server process dies on import:

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp.server.fastmcp'. This is mcp 2.x, where FastMCP was renamed to MCPServer ...
```

Upstream Blender MCP has no mcp 2 revision to move the pin to (it
constrains `mcp<2`), and Studio cannot go back to mcp 1 because
data-designer and the newer MCP connection handshake need mcp 2.

This change makes the launcher register `mcp.server.fastmcp` as an alias
of `mcp.server.mcpserver` when the installed mcp has no such module,
before the runtime is imported. The runtime only uses `FastMCP(name,
instructions=...)`, `@tool(annotations=...)`, `Image(data=...,
format=...)` and `run(transport="stdio")`, all of which keep the same
signature on `MCPServer`.

One behaviour differs: mcp 2 hides the text of any exception a tool
raises, so the model would only see `Error executing tool
execute_blender_code_for_cli` instead of the Blender traceback, or
`Error executing tool get_objects_summary` instead of "Cannot connect to
Blender ... Ensure Blender is running with the MCP addon enabled". The
aliased `FastMCP` re-raises tool exceptions as `ToolError`, which mcp 2
reports with the same `Error executing tool <name>: <message>` text mcp
1 produced.

With mcp 1 installed the alias is never added, so nothing changes there.
The Blender MCP setup flow and UI are unchanged.

### Testing

Pinned runtime (`4309a39`, checksum-verified archive) launched through
`launcher.py` over stdio, listed and called through a fastmcp client
against a fake Blender bridge socket:

| Environment | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| mcp 2.3.0, fastmcp 4.1.6 (current Studio) | `ModuleNotFoundError: No
module named 'mcp.server.fastmcp'`, connection closed | 23 tools listed,
`get_screenshot_of_window_as_json` returns JSON,
`get_screenshot_of_window_as_image` returns an `image/png` ImageContent
with the exact bytes |
| mcp 1.30.0, fastmcp 2.14.7 | 23 tools, both calls work | same, alias
not used |

Parity: the same harness on mcp 1.30.0 and on mcp 2.3.0 with this change
gives byte-identical output (17709 bytes) for all 23 tool input / output
schemas, annotations and descriptions, successful JSON, image and
`execute_blender_code` calls, bridge errors, invalid arguments, and
Blender not running.

New test `test_launcher_runs_v1_fastmcp_runtime_on_installed_mcp` runs
the launcher on a stub runtime written against the v1 API and checks a
failing tool's error text. It fails on main with mcp 2
(`ModuleNotFoundError`), fails with only the plain alias (`'Error
executing tool fail'`), and passes with this change on both mcp 1 and
mcp 2.

code 1." Unsloth installs Codex only when it is missing and never
updates it, so anyone who installed Codex before late May kept hitting
this on every launch, including with `--as-subagent` and `--auto-route`.

Now `unsloth start codex` checks the installed Codex version before
loading anything. When it is older than 0.134.0, it offers to update it
with the same consent prompt used to install a missing agent, then
re-checks the version before launching:

- An npm install is updated in its own prefix (`npm install -g --prefix
<that prefix> @openai/codex@latest`), so the updated copy is the one
that resolves. Installing into `~/.local` instead would leave an older
copy earlier on PATH in front, and the same error would come back.
- A Homebrew install is updated with `brew upgrade codex`.
- The update runs through the agent installer, so a Studio install that
only has the bundled Node/npm works too, and on Windows the
PowerShell-quoted command is kept verbatim (paths such as `O'Brien`
survive).
- Any other install (standalone binary, other package managers) gets no
automatic update: Unsloth names the old copy and asks to update it the
way it was installed, or remove it so `unsloth start codex` installs a
current one.

Without a TTY, or when the update is declined, it stops with "Codex
0.134.0 or newer is needed" and the update command. Codex 0.134.0 and
newer launch as before. When the version cannot be read, or with
`--no-launch` and `--app`, nothing changes.

Verified with real Codex 0.133.0 / 0.134.0 installs: 0.133.0 fails on
the profile and 0.134.0 does not; following the printed command for a
global npm install upgrades the copy that resolves (0.133.0 to 0.167.0);
the accepted in-place update does the same through the installer.
`unsloth_cli/tests/test_start.py` passes on Linux, macOS and Windows.

Studio: ask before Python runs blocked shell commands via __import__ (#16840)

In Auto and Off permission modes, a Python tool call like `import os;
os.system("rm -rf ~")` shows an approval card, but the same command
written as `__import__('os').system("rm -rf ~")` ran straight away with
no card. The same gap covered `importlib.import_module('os')`,
`sys.modules['os']`, `import posix` or `import nt`, a name bound to
`os.system` or `subprocess.run` (`f = os.system; f(...)`), and a
Terminal `python3 -c` one-liner using any of these. Where no OS sandbox
sits behind the check (Docker, Linux without bwrap, Windows without the
container, or Sandbox set to Low), that command ran on the host.

The shell command check now recognises the os and subprocess modules
when they are reached in these ways, so these forms get the same
treatment as the plain `import os` form: a blocked or non-literal
command asks for approval and is refused if it still reaches execution.
Ordinary calls such as `__import__('os').getcwd()` or `os.system('ls')`
behave as before.

Studio chat UI test: wait for the monitor size limits before the resize, and report them (#16885)

## Summary

Follow-up to #16861, whose retry did not fix the Linux `Chat UI Tests
(chat)` failure in the floating monitor check:

```
[ui] resize stopped at 260x141, dragging the grip again
[ui] resize stopped at 256x141, dragging the grip again
AssertionError: [ui] FAIL: resize width: expected 296, got 256
```

Since #16861 merged it failed 4 of 12 completed `Unsloth UI CI` runs,
including main (run 42159942657), and all three drags ended at 256-260
px wide with the height unchanged. So the pointer was not losing steps,
as #16861 assumed. The box would not grow at all.

256 px is the panel's natural width (`minWidth` in
`useFloatingPanelLayout`), and 260 px is the narrow viewport the check
sets just before the resize (`{"width": 260, "height": 400}`). That
points at the panel's `maxWidth`/`maxHeight` still holding the narrow
viewport's values when the resize starts. CSS `min-width` then wins and
pins the box. The limits only follow the viewport through a
`ResizeObserver` on a CPU-throttled page, and `wait_for_box("viewport
restore", ...)` passes as soon as the 256 px box fits, without waiting
for the limits.

`tests/studio/playwright_chat_ui.py`, the resize step only:

- remove #16861's retry loop;
- before the drag, wait up to 5 s for the monitor's computed `max-width`
/ `max-height` to allow the target size;
- if they never do, fail with the computed min/max width and height and
the inline style. That would be a real layout bug: the panel cannot be
resized after the window was narrowed;
- if the drag still lands short, log the same limits before the existing
assertions.

The size and position assertions are unchanged.

Studio GGUF: fuse Q8_0 dequant and cast into one kernel (LTX-2.5 Q8_0 denoise -12%, bit-identical) (#16884)

## Summary

GGUF Q8_0 denoisers (LTX-2.5 Q8_0 is the measured case) spent a large
part of every forward dequantizing weights. Studio compiles diffusers'
`dequantize_gguf_tensor`, but `GGUFLinear.forward_native` then casts the
fp16 result to the compute dtype in a separate eager copy. For Q8_0 the
compiled dequant itself also splits into three kernels, because
`d.view(float16)` on a non-contiguous byte slice cannot fuse. That is 4
kernels per Q8_0 Linear per forward instead of 1.

This PR dequantizes and casts Q8_0 weights in one compiled kernel. The
dequantized weights are bit-identical to the stock path, so frames do
not change.

## What / why / evidence

**What.** `diffusion_gguf_compile.py`:
- **`_q8_0_blocks_dequant_cast`** views the contiguous Q8_0 bytes as
int16 (scale) and int8 (codes) before slicing, so nothing is copied out.
It computes `d * q` in the same order as diffusers, then casts.
- **fp16 rounding is kept.** If inductor fused the product and the cast
directly, it would round the fp32 product straight to bf16 and skip the
fp16 rounding step. On random blocks about 25% of words then differ. An
int16 bitcast plus `& -1` forces the fp16 rounding inside the kernel; in
eager mode it does nothing.
- **Install.** `install_compiled_dequant` patches
`GGUFLinear.forward_native` with the same gating as the compiled
dequant. Only 2-D Q8_0 weights with a compute dtype take the fused path.
Every other quant type (Q4_K and the rest) takes the stock forward
unchanged.
- **Off switch.** `uninstall_compiled_dequant` reverts the patch, and
`UNSLOTH_DIFFUSION_GGUF_FUSED_Q8_0=0` disables it.

**Why.** On the LTX-2.5 Q8_0 profile (G4, resident), the denoise window
spent copy_cast 1.89 s + elementwise 0.79 s + triton 0.60 s per 5
forwards in weight dequant, next to 3.3 s of bf16 GEMMs.

**Evidence. LTX-2.5 Q8_0 GGUF, 1280x704x121, two-stage distilled, whole
card (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, Colab G4).** Base = main b75a4cd721, head
= this branch, one VM, arm order S F F S, 2 new prompts per arm:

| | base S1 / S2 | head F1 / F2 |
|---|---|---|
| denoise s / clip (median) | 11.98 / 11.97 | 10.58 / 10.57 |
| step s (phase median) | 0.616 / 0.616 | 0.488 / 0.485 |
| steady s / clip | 13.36 / 13.39 | 11.96 / 11.96 |
| frames md5 (v0, v1) | e91bd8c6b0, fdeea50dc9 | e91bd8c6b0, fdeea50dc9
|

- **Speed.** Denoise -11.7% and steady clip -10.5%. A/A spread is 0.1%
on base and 0.0% on head.
- **Frames.** Bit-identical between base and head: every frame matches,
PSNR 99 dB, LPIPS 0.
- **Per-Linear microbench (A100, 5 interleaved repeats).** Weight
dequant + cast for 4096x4096: 0.345 ms to 0.124 ms. For 16384x4096:
1.270 ms to 0.205 ms. The head forward at M=3520 is within 3-10% of a
plain bf16 GEMM.

## Tests

New `studio/backend/tests/test_diffusion_gguf_fused_q8_0.py`. On base 15
of its 17 tests fail; on head all 17 pass.
- **Bit identity:** words match diffusers' eager dequant + cast for real
`gguf` Q8_0 blocks and for random bytes (fp16 overflow, subnormals,
NaN). Covered for bf16 / fp16 / fp32 outputs, eager and compiled, with
`emulate_precision_casts` off and on.
- **The bitcast is needed:** a naive fusion is shown to differ.
- **Forward:** the patched forward matches the stock forward bit for bit
and never calls the stock dequant.
- **Other quant types:** Q4_K still takes the stock forward.
- **Compile:** `torch._dynamo.explain` gives 0 graph breaks and 1 graph;
4 layer shapes compile once each (dynamic).
- **Switches:** uninstall and the env kill switch both work.

With `test_diffusion_gguf_compile.py`, `test_diffusion_speed.py` and
`test_diffusion_autoopt_parity.py`, everything passes.

## Not proven

- **Torch versions:** only torch 2.12 (CPU) and 2.13 / 2.14 (GPU) were
exercised. Not tested on the torch 2.6 floor.
- **Untouched paths:** the max-tier block-compile path (the patch is not
installed there) and `DIFFUSERS_GGUF_CUDA_KERNELS=1` (`forward_cuda`).
- **Other quant types:** Q4_K and the other K-quants keep the stock
compiled dequant. That path already differs from eager in its fp16
rounding, so fusing them is a separate decision.
- **Other cards:** only the G4 (Blackwell) and A100 were measured.

Load path: read an adapter's base config through the probe memo, skip the remote mapper for unknown LoRA bases in Studio (#16793)

Two repeated lookups on the LoRA load path.

## 1. `FastModel.from_pretrained`: adapter base config read through the
probe memo

When an adapter is loaded through `FastModel` (Gemma 3 / 4, Qwen-VL,
gpt-oss and other `FastModel` families, and Studio LoRA loads), the
diffusion dispatch check read the base model's config with a direct
`AutoConfig.from_pretrained` call. The probes just before and after it
in the same load already ask for the same config through
`_memo_config_probe`, so this one repeated the `config.json` HEAD and
the resolve-cache HEAD on every adapter load.

It now goes through `_memo_config_probe` with the same arguments and the
same `except Exception` fallback. The memo's existing rules apply
unchanged: it returns a copy, and never stores `trust_remote_code`
results or errors.

Local LoRA on a tiny Gemma 3 Hub base:

| | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP requests per load, with a token | 7 | 5 |
| HTTP requests per load, without a token | 9 | 7 |
| `AutoConfig` calls, with / without a token | 3 / 4 | 2 / 3 |

The saved probe costs 85 ms median online here (53 to 143 ms, n = 10);
on a home connection at 150 ms per request it is about 300 ms per
adapter load. The final weight-load call and the order of the load
events are identical in all 20 runs, and a missing base raises the same
error with the same text.

## 2. Studio worker: skip the remote mapper for a LoRA base the
installed mapper does not know

`_load_download_repos` (which lists the repos a load will download)
called `get_model_name(base)` for every LoRA base. For a base that is
not in the installed mapper tables, that fetches and parses `mapper.py`
from GitHub, and the answer is either the base itself (already in the
list) or an exception (ignored), so the repo list never changes. The
load then fetches the remote mapper again on its own. The worker now
calls `get_model_name` only for names in the installed mapper tables or
`BAD_MAPPINGS` (the check `_loader_repo` in
`core/inference/inference.py` makes, except that `BAD_MAPPINGS` names
still go through the mapper here, as on main). Any other base resolves
to itself, so the pre-quantized suffix strip applied when
`ALLOW_PREQUANTIZED_MODELS` is off (AMD Instinct on bitsandbytes <
0.49.2) still lists the stripped repo the loader downloads.

Saves one GitHub GET per Studio LoRA load with such a base: 58 ms median
here (40 to 89 ms, n = 5), and seconds when GitHub is slow.

## Tests

- New
`tests/python/test_load_probe_memo.py::test_fastmodel_adapter_load_probes_base_config_once`
(string token and `False`): fails on main, passes here, on transformers
4.57.6 and 5.22.1. A missing-base case passes on both and keeps the same
error.
- New
`studio/backend/tests/test_load_download_repos_mapper.py::test_unmapped_lora_base_skips_the_remote_mapper`:

- `studio/backend/tests/test_load_downloads.py`: its loader stub gained

- 51 neighbouring test files (about 2950 tests): the same 10

Studio: decode the Transformers chat stream incrementally instead of re-decoding the current line per token (#16800)

The Transformers chat backend streams through transformers'
`TextIteratorStreamer` (directly, or via
`ReasoningTextIteratorStreamer`, which only overrides
`on_finalized_text`). Upstream `put` re-decodes every token since the
last newline on each new token, so the per-token cost grows with the
length of the current line: long single-line output such as JSON
tool-call arguments, CJK prose without newlines or long paragraphs gets
slower token by token. On tool turns `NativeToolTokenDecoder.decode`
additionally rebuilds a filtered id list over that whole cache each
time. This runs on the generate thread, inside the decode loop.

## Change

- New `IncrementalTextIteratorStreamer`
(`core/inference/incremental_streamer.py`): the same `put` logic as
upstream (skip prompt, newline flush, CJK flush, last-space split,
`on_finalized_text`), but once the current line reaches 64 ids it is
decoded through `IncrementalDecode`, or
`NativeToolTokenDecoder.incremental()` on tool turns, which the MLX path
already uses. Shorter lines, where upstream's whole-line decode is
cheaper, and tokenizers the incremental decoder does not support keep
upstream `put` unchanged.
- The line decoder is built once per streamer and reset where upstream
clears `token_cache` (after a newline and in `end()`). Detection keys on
upstream rebinding `token_cache`, so no upstream method is overridden
besides `put`.
- `split_profile` keys its cache on the base vocab size plus the
added-token count instead of `len(tokenizer)`: on tokenizers < 0.23 (the
transformers 4.57 stack) `len()` rebuilds the whole vocab, 22 to 116 ms
per call on Qwen3, Llama-3.2 and Gemma-3. This also speeds up the MLX
path's per-request decoder setup.
- `ReasoningTextIteratorStreamer` inherits from the new class, and the
three plain `TextIteratorStreamer` call sites in `inference.py` (text
path, Harmony fallback, audio) use it. Upstream `put` is the same in
transformers 4.57.6 and 5.22.1 (only `cast(str, ...)` differs).

## Results

`put` cost per token on real tokenizers (median of 5 ABBA-interleaved
runs, CPU, ratios only since the host was loaded):

| Tokenizer | Path | Text | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3 | plain | 4,096-token single line | 0.56 ms | 0.013 ms |
| Qwen3 | tool decoder | 4,096-token single line | 1.34 ms | 0.018 ms |
| Qwen3 | plain | 2,048 tokens, CJK | 0.41 ms | 0.036 ms |
| Llama-3.2 | plain | 4,096-token single line | 1.66 ms | 0.050 ms |
| Gemma-3 | tool decoder | 4,096-token single line | 6.75 ms | 0.097 ms
|
| all three | both | 2,048 tokens, a newline every ~20 tokens | 0.009 to
0.039 ms | 0.009 to 0.039 ms (upstream `put`) |

An earlier revision built a new decoder per line, which made
newline-heavy text 2 to 7 ms per token; the threshold and the single
decoder fix that, and a test now pins it.

## Parity

- Exact chunk sequence (every `(text, stream_end)` call) equal to
upstream `put` in all 18 benchmark cells above, and in the parity tests
on transformers 4.57.6 and 5.22.1.
- Real `model.generate` on tiny Qwen3 and tiny Llama (1,500 sampled
tokens, 3 seeds, plain / tools / reasoning streamers): identical
generated ids, chunks and streamed text against upstream `put`, with the
incremental path engaged.

## Tests

- `tests/test_incremental_streamer.py` (26 tests): chunk parity on
in-memory tokenizers (asserting the incremental path engaged on long
lines), a bounded-work check that upstream `put` fails, and a check that
the decoder is resolved once per streamer and never for short lines.
- 11 streaming, tool-token, stop-sequence, Harmony and refactor-guard
test files: 402 passed, 0 failed on both main and this branch, on
transformers 4.57.6 and 5.22.1.

Unsloth Studio: keep chat search fast on long histories by not shipping tool images and widget seeds to the index (#16848)

## What was wrong

Chat search builds its index from the newest 200 chats with one `POST
/api/chat/messages:batch` request (`view: "search"`). The search view
drops metadata and media parts, but it passes tool-call parts through
whole, so python images, MCP image envelopes and MCP Apps widget seeds
still ride along, even though the index throws them away in the browser.

On a long history that one response gets bigger than the longest string
V8 can hold (`0x1fffffe8` chars), so reading it fails. The `.catch` in
`buildChatSearchIndex` then treats every chat as missing and falls back
to two full-view requests per chat (400 in all), carrying every image
and metadata blob. Reported in the Discord help thread: search sometimes
takes over 5 minutes to find a chat.

Code at the base commit `a17bfe91ab`:
-
[`routes/chat_history.py#L1707-L1723`](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/blob/a17bfe91ab6e064b72223b770b14a54863c4dceb/studio/backend/routes/chat_history.py#L1707-L1723):
tool-call parts are kept as stored
-
[`use-chat-search-index.ts#L198-L222`](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/blob/a17bfe91ab6e064b72223b770b14a54863c4dceb/studio/frontend/src/features/chat/hooks/use-chat-search-index.ts#L198-L222):
one request for all 200 chats, then the per-chat fallback on any failure

## Changes in this PR

- The search view trims each tool-call part to what `searchableText`
reads: keys it skips (`images`, `audio`, `video`, `*b64*`), values
nested past the depth it stops at, a widget result's UI seed, the image
tails after `__IMAGES__` or a valid `__MCP_IMAGES__` envelope, and
inline `data:...;base64,...` URLs. Bare base64 runs with no `data:`
prefix are left for the browser to strip, since scanning for them in
Python costs far more per character. A string is only trimmed when the
browser would read the trimmed copy back the same, so the built index
doesn't change.
- The index asks for messages 20 chats at a time, so no single response
has to hold the whole index, and a failed read only falls back for those
20.

## Before / after

MacBook Pro (Apple M5, 32 GB), Unsloth Studio served from each commit,
scratch store of 300 chats (about 40 messages each, 1.9 GB of messages:
reasoning, python output, file reads, web search, MCP widget results,
images in some tool results). Open chat search, Chats tab, wait until
all 300 chats are listed.

| | base `a17bfe91ab` | this PR `be3d387473` (measured before
`a613896fcf`, which only trims data URLs further) |
|---|---|---|
| batch response for the newest 200 chats | 1235 MB, cannot be read as a
string | 484 MB in 10 requests |
| per-chat fallback reads | 200 (400 requests) | 0 |
| open to index ready, 3 runs | 15.7 s once, tab crashed twice | 6.1 s,
9.2 s, 7.7 s |

![Chat search on a 300-chat, 1.9 GB history. BEFORE (a17bfe91ab): all
300 chats listed after 9.9 s, 1 batch request that failed to parse and
200 per-chat fallback reads. AFTER (a613896fcf): listed in 6.2 s, 10
batch requests, no fallback
reads](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LeoBorcherding/unsloth/3ec758ee7c07570216816909dd06e05bd9849923/pr/744/chat_search_before_after.png)

Taken with the pr-ui-evidence driver (scene `chat_search_index`),
headless Chromium on a MacBook Pro (Apple M5), one fresh install per
side. The scene writes the same seeded history into each home, opens
chat search on the Chats tab and waits for every chat to be listed. The
caption is drawn by the harness. Two runs: BEFORE 14.1 s and 9.9 s,
AFTER 6.7 s and 6.2 s, with 200 vs 0 per-chat fallback reads both times.
Neither headless BEFORE run crashed; the two crashes in the table were
in a desktop browser tab.

Node, same store: base fails with `Cannot create a string longer than
0x1fffffe8 characters`; this PR builds the index in 2.1 s. On a lighter
2000-chat store (1 GB), the build stays at about 55 ms and the response
drops from 44.8 MB to 23.3 MB.

## How it was tested

- The built index is byte-identical between the full view, the old
search view and the new one, on the 2000-chat store and on five fuzz
stores built to hit every trim rule (binary keys at every depth, widget
and non-widget results, valid and invalid image envelopes, both markers
in either order, data URLs with whitespace that JavaScript and Python
classify differently), rerun at `a613896fcf`.
- New tests: `test_chat_search_view.py` (trim rules, widget results,
strings left alone) and `chat-search-text.test.ts` (requests go out 20
chats at a time). The behaviour tests fail on base.
- Frontend `tsc -b`, `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` and `npm test` (14,925
of 14,926 passed, 0 failed).
- Backend `test_chat_search_view.py`, `test_chat_history_routes.py`,
`test_chat_history_storage.py`, `test_chat_message_identity.py`: 260
passed at `a613896fcf`. A wider `-k chat` run has 90 failures that fail
the same way on base, plus one timing test that fails only under load

## Not tested

- Windows and Unsloth Desktop. The failure is in the browser's string

foreground. That delete is a silent 40 s on x64 and 30 s on ARM64
(measured in the earlier update profiling as the gap between "Setup
Complete" and the next line), during which the installer, or Desktop's
update screen, just waits.

## Change

`Complete-StudioVenvRollback` already disarms the restore paths before
it deletes the tree. Its last step now hands the delete to a separate
hidden process:

- A plain `powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command <text>` is
started with no window (no encoded command, no execution-policy
override).
- The tree is renamed (same volume, atomic) to
`unsloth_studio.rollback.<stamp>.<deleter PID>`, the name format the
existing `Remove-StaleStudioVenvRollbacks` sweep already handles: it
leaves a tree alone while that PID is alive, and removes it on a later
run if the deleter was stopped early (for example when Desktop's job
object ends). `uninstall.ps1` also matches `rollback.*`.
- If starting the process or the rename fails, nothing has changed and
the installer deletes in the foreground exactly as before, so output,
exit code, venv contents and restore-on-failure behaviour are unchanged
in every case. The only visible difference is that the disk space comes
back a little later.
- The child is started through the shell without inherited handles, so a
caller reading the installer's stdout / stderr (Desktop) is not held
open by it.

to the Windows leg of `cross-platform-parity-ci.yml`, runs under both

returns (the pipe is not held), a sweep during the delete prints nothing

## Summary

`Source lint` and `workflow-trigger lint` have been failing on main
since #16806 (`306aad9c25`), so every PR inherits them. For example
#16891, which only touches Qwen-Image-2.1 diffusion code:

```
unsloth/models/rl_replacements.py:95  compile(...) is handed a value that is not written out
FAILED tests/security/test_lint_exec_literals.py::test_the_baseline_matches_the_tree_it_was_recorded_against
```

#16806 is correct. To decide whether the lines above a class can be
skipped, it checks that they form complete statements. It does that with
`compile(source, "<unsloth_class_source>", "exec", ast.PyCF_ONLY_AST)`,
which only builds a syntax tree and never runs anything.
`scripts/lint_exec_literals.py` flags every `exec`, `eval` or `compile`
whose argument is not a literal, and that call was not in

ast.PyCF_ONLY_AST)` becomes `ast.parse(..., "<unsloth_class_source>",

call. It returns the same tree and raises the same `SyntaxError`, which
is all the loop catches. It is not one of the lint's sinks, so the
baseline stays as it is and does not need a hand-written exemption.

Studio RAG: batch llama-server token counts and encode the auto-inject query once (#16812)

Two repeated round trips in Studio RAG.

## 1. llama-server token counts, one `/tokenize` POST per text

When the RAG embedder is the llama-server backend (auto-picked when
there is no CUDA / ROCm GPU: macOS, CPU-only and Intel machines), its
token counter only had a single-text form, so chunking a document fell
back to one `/tokenize` POST for every page, split piece, merged chunk
and overlap text. Deep research web ranking uses the same counter per
page.

`/tokenize` in llama.cpp accepts an array for `content`: it tokenizes
each string on its own exactly as it would a lone string and copies
integers through. The counter now has a `many` form that sends up to 256
texts (at most 262,144 characters) per POST with a `-1` marker between
them and splits the reply on the markers. If a build refuses the array
(error status) or the reply has the wrong number of markers, that
counter goes back to one POST per text. Single counts send the same
request as before. The per-text memo (4,096 entries), `_serve_lock`,
readiness, restarts and the CPU fallback are unchanged; each batch POST
holds the lock only for that POST, so a query encode never waits for a
whole document.

CPU llama-server with bge-small f16 (Linux, 5 repeats per side, each
side run twice):

| Document | POSTs on main | POSTs here | Chunking time on main | here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100-page PDF | 4,403 | 23 | 2.32 / 2.44 s | 0.18 / 0.14 s |
| 77-page PDF | 4,761 | 23 | 2.66 to 3.25 s | 0.14 to 0.19 s |
| 15-page PDF | 699 | 6 | | |
| CJK article | 202 | 6 | | |
| markdown | 350 | 14 | | |

Chunks are byte-identical in all 150 cells: 5 tokenizers (bge WordPiece,
Llama SPM, SmolLM2 GPT-2 BPE, Gemma 3 SPM, Qwen3 BPE) x 6 documents (3
PDFs, CJK, markdown, and an adversarial file with special tokens, emoji
ZWJ sequences, `\r\n` and empty pages) x 5 chunk size / overlap
settings.

## 2. Auto-injected context encoded the same query up to twice

`build_rag_autoinject` can search with the same query more than once in
one turn (thread retrieval, the lexical-then-hybrid retry, the dense
probe), and each search encoded the query again. It now runs inside
`retrieval.query_vector_memo()`, as compaction recall already does. Over
a 1,728-scenario matrix (knowledge base, thread, project, auto-inject on
/ off, retrieval mode, score floor, whole-document, context length,
query) the injected context is identical (apart from the random tool
call id), and query encodes drop from 844 to 796: the 48 scenarios that
encoded twice now encode once.

## Tests

- New `tests/test_rag_llama_token_batch.py` (12 tests): 11 fail on main
(batching, marker split, fallback on refusal and on a marker-count
mismatch, memo, auto-inject encode count); the 12th checks a failed POST
still raises.
- 60 neighbouring RAG, web rank, recall and compaction test files: 2,107
passed on main, 2,119 here (the new file), 24 skipped on both, 0
failures.

back to one POST per text.

Studio: index FK child columns, partial index for the run lease sweep, keep the inventory clean on Deep Research start (#16795)

Three hot spots in `studio.db`, all inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (so they
hold the writer lock while they run).

## 1. Foreign-key child columns without an index

`foreign_keys=ON` is set on every connection, and these columns
reference `chat_messages(id)` / `chat_threads(id)` with `ON DELETE
CASCADE` / `SET NULL`, but had no index:

- `chat_generation_runs.user_message_id`,
`chat_generation_runs.assistant_message_id`
- `research_runs.thread_id`, `.user_message_id`, `.assistant_message_id`
- `scheduled_task_runs.thread_id`

So every deleted chat message scanned the whole `chat_generation_runs`
table twice (one row per chat turn, each carrying its full
`request_json`). That cost lands on thread delete, project delete,
message sync that prunes messages, and clear-all. These are the only FK
child columns without an index (checked with `foreign_key_list` on every
table); `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` goes from `SCAN` to `SEARCH ... USING
COVERING INDEX` for all six.

## 2. Partial index for the run lease sweep

The reconcile sweep (`WHERE status IN ('queued','running','cancelling')
ORDER BY created_at, id`, every 60 s per account and once per account at
startup) had no index starting with `status`, so it read every row,
including the `request_json` overflow pages. A partial index on
`(created_at, id)` with that exact status list now serves it, same rows
in the same order (precedent: the existing partial index in
`_ensure_schema`).

## 3. Deep Research start rebuilt the whole attachment inventory

Inserting the Deep Research assistant placeholder fired the inventory
trigger that marks the attachment inventory dirty, so the next message
upsert or sync rebuilt the entire inventory (delete everything, re-read
and JSON-parse every message). Chat generation already avoids this for
its own placeholder with an `inventory_was_clean` guard (#14217). The
research placeholder (`'[]'`, no attachments) now uses the same guard;
an inventory that was already dirty stays dirty.

## Results

Synthetic `studio.db`: 40 threads x 150 messages, 2,999 chat runs with
30 KB `request_json`, 200 research runs, 600 scheduled task runs; warm
cache; 3 runs per arm, main run twice as A/A. After every operation all
tables were dumped and compared: identical on main and this branch.

| Operation | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear all chats | about 38 s (34 to 47 s; A/A 36 to 41 s) | 0.58 to
0.76 s |
| Delete one 150-message thread | 2.6 to 3.8 s | 0.02 to 0.17 s |
| Message sync that prunes 20 messages | 0.53 to 1.57 s | 26 to 32 ms |
| Lease sweep (every 60 s) | 21 to 37 ms | under 0.1 ms |
| First sync after a Deep Research start | 0.40 to 0.54 s | 20 to 53 ms
|

One-time cost: building the new indexes when this branch first opens an
existing database takes 0.6 to 0.7 s at 3k runs and 1.4 s on a 1.8 GB
database with 50k runs (inside `_ensure_schema` at startup).
`_ensure_schema` stays idempotent (a second run takes 2 to 4 ms and
leaves `sqlite_master` unchanged), and an older build opening a database
this branch already indexed starts normally.

The two `fetchone()` lookups without `ORDER BY` that now use the
`assistant_message_id` index still return the same row: `create_run`
refuses to bind a second run to an assistant message that already has
one.

## Tests

- New `tests/test_studio_db_hot_path_indexes.py` (5 tests): 3 fail on
main (one per item), all pass here.
- 20 neighbouring storage, chat generation, chat history, research and
scheduled task test files: 1,385 passed, 0 failed on this branch.

## Not covered

- Cold-cache timings (on main the sweep and the deletes read more from
disk, so the real gap is larger) and Windows / macOS file systems.

RL patch pass: skip the whole-module ast.parse when reading trainer class source on Python < 3.13 (#16806)

On Python 3.9 to 3.12, `inspect.getsource(<class>)` parses the class's
whole module with `ast.parse` and walks the tree to find the class, on
every call (3.13 jumps straight to the recorded line instead). The RL
patch pass reads the source of every TRL trainer and config class it
rewrites, plus `UnslothEfficientGRPO` from the 250 KB
`unsloth_zoo/rl_replacements.py`. `PatchFastRL` runs at module level in
`llama.py`, so this is paid on every `import unsloth` on a GPU host,
SFT-only users included; Colab is on Python 3.12.

## Change

`_class_source(cls)` in `unsloth/models/rl_replacements.py`, used for
the 5 class lookups in `rl.py` and for `UnslothEfficientGRPO`. On Python
3.13+ it is `inspect.getsource`. On older versions it finds the class by
its single `class <Name>` line in the module's linecache lines, steps up
over plain single-line decorators, and returns `inspect.getblock` from
there, the same lines `inspect.getsource` returns. It falls back to
`inspect.getsource` for anything ambiguous: a nested qualname, zero or
several definitions of the name (indented ones included, so a
`TYPE_CHECKING` stub keeps `inspect`'s answer), multi-line or separated
decorators, preceding lines that do not compile as complete statements,
a class whose own methods are not inside the found block (or that has
none), or any exception.

## Results (Python 3.12.3)

| | `inspect.getsource` | `_class_source` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the 35 class lookups of the RL patch pass (median of 7, outputs
asserted equal) | 401 ms | 183 ms |
| inside the patch pass, 5 alternating runs (base A/A 0.29 to 0.42 s) |
0.453 s median | 0.205 s median |
| `UnslothEfficientGRPO` alone | 50 ms | 2.3 ms |

About 0.22 s saved per process on 3.12. Python 3.13 is unchanged (165 ms
vs 165 ms).

## Parity

- Generated `Unsloth*Trainer.py` files byte-identical on main and this
branch: TRL 0.25.1 + transformers 4.57.6 (16 trainers), TRL 1.17.1 +
transformers 4.57.6 (14), TRL 1.17.1 + transformers 5.22.1 (14), on 3.12
and 3.13.
- Independent check of every class in every importable module of
transformers 5.22.1 (14,714 classes), 4.57.6 (9,806), TRL 1.17.1 and
0.25.1: no difference from `inspect.getsource`. 36 adversarial cases
(names inside strings, duplicate and conditional definitions, decorators
with arguments over several lines, comments between decorator and class,
classes without methods, CRLF, tabs, unicode names) match or fall back.

## Tests

- New `tests/test_rl_class_source.py` (21 tests): parity for every TRL
trainer / config class and `UnslothEfficientGRPO`, the fast path
actually taken for SFT / GRPO / DPO, synthetic decorated / duplicate /

Studio: let unsloth start dsh install DeepSeek Harness on Node 22 (#16844)

On a first run without dsh, `unsloth start dsh` offers to install it
with `npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh`. Every published dsh version is a
prerelease, and the current `latest` (0.2.2-rc.1) asks for Node 24.9 or
newer. With a bare package name npm skips that release on older Node,
finds no stable version to fall back to, and stops with `ETARGET No
matching version found`. So anyone on Node 22 LTS gets a failed install,
and the printed "run it yourself" command fails the same way.

The install command now asks for `@deepseek-ai/dsh@latest`, which npm
installs with only an engine warning, and the installed dsh starts and
talks to Studio on Node 22. The agent guides CI installs dsh with the
same command, since it runs on Node 22 too.

This depends on the npm registry: it started with the 2026-11-04 dsh
release, and a stable dsh release would also make the bare name resolve
again. The `@latest` form keeps working either way.

Chroma1-HD's ComfyUI fp8 file (`Comfy-Org/Chroma1-HD`
`Chroma1-HD-fp8mixed`) ran 1.85x slower per step in Studio than in
ComfyUI. #16710 denied every activation-quantizing scheme for Chroma, so

RTX 6000 Ada, 1024², 26 steps, CFG 3.5 (two passes per step), lower is
better:

| | Before (main) | After (this PR) | ComfyUI v0.44.0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seconds per step | 1.65 | 0.94 | 0.89 |

get_chat_template: apply mapping when the role key is not renamed (#16425)

`get_chat_template(..., mapping = {"role": "role", "user": "human", "assistant": "gpt"})` silently ignored the mapping: Llama 3.1 wrote `human`/`gpt` as headers and ChatML turned every turn into a system turn. Mapping only `content` (e.g. `"text"`) raised `UndefinedError`.

Cause: the ShareGPT conversion is wrapped in `if 'role' not in messages[0]`, hardcoded to the default key, so any mapping that keeps `role` skipped it.

Each turn takes its content from the mapped content key when it has one and otherwise keeps its own fields, so content-less tool-call turns and canonical histories passed with a content-only mapping render as before. Standard role/content messages with a mapping that renames `role` still skip it, and the default mapping adds no wrapper at all.

Tests: `tests/python/test_get_chat_template_sharegpt_mapping.py` covers role-kept mappings, content-only mappings, a ShareGPT history that opens with a content-less tool call, and a canonical tool-call-first history under a content-only mapping; the new cases fail on main or on the earlier revision of this PR and pass now (30/30). 313 neighbouring chat-template tests pass on both main and this branch. Studio audio analyze: screen the true peak in float32 and convolve only the candidate outputs (#16794)

`POST /api/inference/audio/analyze` measures the true peak (BS.1770
Annex 2, 4x oversampling) by running `np.convolve` for each of the 4
polyphase filters over every chunk of every channel and taking the
largest absolute output. That is the slowest part of the analysis after
loudness: about 3.3 s of a 7.6 to 8.3 s analysis for a 10-minute 48 kHz
stereo clip.

## Change

Per chunk, a cheap float32 screen (12 multiply-adds per output, plain
numpy ufuncs) estimates every oversampled output, with a proven error
bound. Only the outputs whose screened value could still be the maximum
(within twice the bound of the screened top, and not below the running
peak) are then computed with the same `np.convolve` call as before, on a
view of the same window, so each recomputed output is the identical dot
product over the same memory. The returned peak is the same float as
main's.

- Bound: a 12-term float32 sum is within about 14 * 2^-24 * reach *
scale of the exact value whatever the summation order (FMA, blocking);
the code uses 2^-19, about 2x margin.
- Silence, NaN, inf and extreme sample values (scale outside 2^-60 ..
2^60) skip the screen and use main's path unchanged; so do chunks where
the candidates are scattered over more than 128 separate spans.
- The screen uses no BLAS call, so its speed does not depend on the
caller's BLAS thread setting.
- The 11 multiply-add terms per chunk reuse one scratch buffer instead
of allocating a temporary each (about 10% faster than allocating, same
screen values).

## Results

`true_peak` on a 10-minute 48 kHz stereo clip, Linux x86_64 (heavily
loaded shared host, medians):

| | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| this run (3 alternating runs each) | 2.54 s (2.42 to 3.33) | 1.82 s
(1.74 to 4.18) |
| independent review (main run twice as A/A) | 3.35 / 3.27 s | 1.95 s |

| current head on a dedicated Colab CPU High-RAM VM (x86_64, 8 vCPUs, no
other tenant), 5 ABBA rounds, fresh process each, single BLAS thread |
5.97 s (5.70 to 6.41) | 3.38 s (3.01 to 3.97) |

On the dedicated VM the current head is 1.77x faster than main with no
overlap between the arms. The returned value was identical in every run.

## Tests

(random chunk sizes 7 to 4096, PCM 16 / 24-bit, square-wave ties,
isolated impulses, NaN / inf / 3e38 spikes, constants at 2^-61 .. 2^61
and denormals), 0 mismatches.

- New `tests/test_audio_true_peak_screen.py` (6 tests): compares against
a copy of main's implementation over 9 lengths and 4 chunk sizes, and
checks the screen path is actually taken (fails on main).
- Independent fuzz of main vs this implementation: 10,000 cases over 16

at chunk edges, repeated and negated ties, 16 / 24 / 32-bit PCM,
denormals, the 2^-60 / 2^60 edges, NaN / inf, 1e35), 0 mismatches. The
earlier BLAS form of the same screen was also fuzzed with 70,000 cases

Studio: read unread scheduled replies aloud when opened (#16847)

With automatic read aloud on, opening a finished scheduled task's reply
stays silent. The reply comes from saved history, so it never fires the
`thread.runEnd` event that starts automatic read aloud for a live
response.

This reads an unread scheduled result aloud once when its chat is opened
from Recents, the Scheduled page, or a chat URL. Playback waits for the
saved messages to load. Opening the chat clears the unread marker before
the reply is available, so the pending playback is held in the current
tab until the matching chat is ready, and dropped if the user leaves
first.

It stays silent for results already read (after a reload or in another
tab too), results that finish in the background, ordinary chat history,
incomplete replies, and when automatic read aloud is off. On a fresh
page load from a direct URL, the browser's autoplay policy can block
playback; the Read aloud button still works then.

Before and after, merge base (`0ab3f0773d`) vs this PR (`be4756cb59`),
opening an unread result from Recents:

![Before and after: opening an unread scheduled
result](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oobabooga/unsloth/pr-media/pr/studio-scheduled-result-auto-read/scheduled_result_read_aloud-cf1b42cfebb1.png)

Tested in Chromium with its default autoplay policy, using a real
scheduled-task run with Gemma 4 E2B and Kokoro:

- Opening from Recents and from the Scheduled page's Open chat button
played the reply once.
- Reloading or reopening sent no second speech request. A result
finishing in the background stayed silent.
- With automatic read aloud off, opening stayed silent.
- On a fresh direct URL, Chromium blocked playback, and the Read aloud
button then played it.
- With the saved-message response delayed, playback waited for it.
Leaving during the delay cancelled it.

The new `scheduled-result-read-aloud.test.ts` and the related frontend
tests, the typecheck and the production build pass.

Studio: keep fine-tuning jobs in order when a batch starts ahead of them (#16832)

Listing fine-tuning jobs page by page through the OpenAI-compatible API
could skip a job. When two compatible jobs started together as a
Multi-LoRA batch while an older job kept waiting, the waiting job later
started with a newer start time and jumped ahead of the batch in the
history. A client that had already paged past the batch never saw it.

Finished runs are now listed by the time the job was queued, falling
back to the start time for runs that never went through the queue or
predate it. The history keeps the order the jobs were submitted in,
however the batches came out.

Fixes #16720


Follow-up on this branch: queue, live and persisted jobs are ordered in
one pass by creation time, with jobs created in the same second ordered
by when they were queued, then by job ID. Before, those jobs could swap
places when a batch moved from running to history, and a client could
skip one. History is still read lazily: a short page reads only the rows
it needs, even after a long backlog. Regression tests for these cases
come from #16835.
